Heading: Road to respite - Indian Express
Content:
GaMaBhaNa, a script developed by Omkar Joshi has helped promote local languages on the Internet

He might be qualified to have a command over computer languages but that does not take away the affection that he has towards his mother tongue. GaMaBhaNa, a script developed by Omkar Joshi, software professional who has been working as a subject matter expert with Amdocs has been the bloodline for countless writers to express their feelings in their own regional language on the World Wide Web.

"I am a poet myself and I used to write on a website I would not want to name. I advised the authorities to make it available for all in order to promote writing but unfortunately I did not get a reply from them. I thus thought of developing my own script," says Joshi explaining the motive behind the script.

What followed the decision was GaMaBhaNa, a script that is based on Java, which thus supports Internet as well as Mozilla Fire Fox. Joshi makes the technical details easy by adding, "Most of the websites or local language software that have vernacular medium of expressions have a complicated process to follow if someone wants to post a reply. It is very keyboard specific. For instance, if I type a message on my computer in a particular script, on somebody else's computer who does have that script loaded, the message might represent different characters thus changing the meaning of the entire message."

The characteristic of GaMaBhaNa is that it is transliterate which means that one can type the English spelling of the desired local language word and what appears on the screen is the word in that particular language. Currently, the website and the application supports nine different languages like Marathi, Hindi, Bangla, Gujarati, Gurumukhi, Kannada, Malayalam, Odiya, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu and English. "For instance if one goes to gamabhana.com, he or she can select options of languages. Thus if he or she selects Marathi and types the spelling of his or her name using regular English keyboard; what will automatically appear on the screen is the same in Devnagari," says Joshi.

The specialty of Joshi's script is that it is extremely user friendly and at the same time freely available for all. Another advantage is that, it can be used in modes like- online and offline by downloading the script on one's computer. One can also attach the Javascript to a website and thus enable the usage of local language on their website. "It is free for all and there have been countless people and organisations who have been using it for promoting regional languages," adds Joshi. A number of websites are benefited by using GaMaBhaNa in their noble cause of encouraging regional writers, poets and authors. "To name a few, they are- myboli.com, misalpav.com, mr.upakram.com, sureshbhat.in, marathiabhyasparishad.com and so on. In fact, the Nepali section of Wikipedia is also powered by GaMaBhaNa. It is open source, which means anyone, and everyone can get it free of cost. People also call me and ask me for the source code," says Joshi.

The advantage is that users do not need to be technically sound to be able to make use of the script. Added features on the website are the library and editor that assist the user while writing. With people from Maharashtra Mandals in countries like UK and USA making use of GaMaBhaNa, Joshi has surely helped languages cross the borders.

Heading: My Beautiful  Bengal - Indian Express
Content:
The 100 benches flanking the Pashan-Sus Road have transformed a once-unnoticeable stretch into a pedestrian paradise

Ashwin Shetty's roadside tea stall has just had a change of fortune. And all because he shifted its position from under a tree to near one of the 100 odd benches that have popped up at the Pashan-Sus road thanks to the Commonwealth Youth Games. "The only reason my tea did not sell the way it should have is because people did not get a place to sit and enjoy its taste. When these benches were put up I decided that I will shift my tapri near one so that my customers can be benefitted by its presence."

The presence of benches along the entire stretch of the road has not benefitted only Shetty and his patrons. The ones sauntering in the greenery of Pashan-Sus road also vouch for the usefulness of it. Taking a stroll has become a routine affair for Mahesh Pethekar and his wife who live in NCL colony at Pashan-Sus road. "You tend to cover a long way when you take a stroll on this road and when its time to return, you feel like taking some rest before starting off again and that is where these benches come into picture. Earlier my wife and I used to take a walk but that used to be very short because we knew that covering a long stretch again can be a tedious process," shares Pethekar.

Where the residents enjoy the benefits of the benches they also feel that initiatives like these motivate people to walk instead of using automobiles for covering even small distances. Ramesh Pathe, senior citizen and a resident says, " For people of our age such benches are like crutches that help and support us. They also stimulate this healthy habit of walking in us. I now enjoy morning and evening walks because I can stop and take rest whenever I feel like. Earlier when the benches were not there, one could not get a proper place to sit for almost three to four kilometers."

Proving to be happening hangout for the residents, the beautified Pashan-Sus road along with the benches has carved a niche in the locality by becoming an inextricable part of its surroundings. Here's a hope of more roads donning a similar picturesque cum practical avtaar in other parts of the city, even if the CYG urgency and impetus is not there anymore.

Heading: The Artist’s Way - Indian Express
Content:
Creativity and the arts hold a special position in Bengal as does nostalgia

Bengal has often been referred to as the cradle of civilisation, an ideal that has been challenged by the likes of Amrita Sher-Gil and Francis Newton Souza. Artists who believed in looking forward and embracing Modernism rather than looking back and trying to revive the past as did their contemporaries: the Tagore brothers, sNandilal Bose and B B Mukherjee.

Bengali artists eventually moved towards Modernism and names like the late Paritosh Sen and Sakti Burman have the status of being seen as international artists. Be that as it may, art from Bengal is arguably born from the soil of its motherland and often falls into the construct of being provincial in an age of globalisation. A case in point is the current exhibition Creative Expressions, a group show by 10 artists from different regions of India.

The pervading themes in this exhibition are mythology, dynasty, fantasy and the genre painting of everyday life in the streets of Kolkata. Dhiren Sasmal, a prominent artist from Kolkata whose pen and ink and mixed media works capture the effervescence of youth says, "I have always been keen to portray my immediate reality. If that makes me provincial then so be it. I cannot talk of events and matters that are distant and not my reality." Ashok Ganguly feels his soft mellow approach to life and romanticism is a product of Bengal that cannot be escaped. "Our soil is soaked with Romanticism and history—it is hard to ignore. However, art is not segmented by boundaries and is timeless. Every artist has his or her own brand and style. Some may want to experiment with the future while others look back at the past and glorifies that," says the artist who believes there is room for all.

Quite in contrast to these romantic voices which crave for the past, painter Samir Aich, who is also showing his work in this exhibition, is a tireless experimenter. "My work seeks to 'figurate' abstract concepts such as the primordial force of nature, or its earthly counterpart, the animal spirit," says Aich. Earlier on, his work depicted these concepts in the shape of a variety of awe-inspiring imagery painted with metallic colours.

The emphasis on the skill of painting and the technicalities of the brush is something that has always been characteristic of Bengali art. Whether the style pursued is surrealistic figuration, like in the instance of the late Bikhash Bhattacharjee or it is the anguished Expressionism of Jogen Choudhury.

The artist Paresh Maity, at the risk of being dubbed a calendar-art lover, still paints beautiful watercolours of land and sea scapes. "Capturing the joy of life and reveling in the sensuousness of life is something very Bengali," says Maity whose wife Jayshree Burman also follows a similar maxim, only in her case mythology figures a lot in her work. As does the work of Tarun Chakraborty, Ananya Banerjee and Debjani Datta.

Their whole point being, that the melding of the modern and the traditional is an inherent part of being Indian.

Heading: What is a found object ? - Indian Express
Content:
Find beauty and the purpose will follow. This is a credo that I try and abide by. Though by no means is it an easy task in cities like Mumbai, where the mind-numbing commute and the daily grind can make one prone to things like road rage.

In Auroville, Pondicherry, the pursuit of beauty, it would seem, is a way of life.

Potters, painters, poets and others of their ilk live and eke out a living in sylvan settings. On the face of it, their lives appear simple and uncluttered; the most common daily routine consists of Tai Chi/Yoga or meditation combined with healthy eating and a work routine that is focused and mindful. It's a routine that is geared to assist the individual and aid the community. The art produced and sold here is beautiful and serene, free of isms and trends, indicative of a spontaneous and free way of thinking and being. This Zen lifestyle is enviable, despite the fact that the community as a whole does suffer from the same ills that plague any settlement.

Walking on dusty tracks and listening to the roar of the blue sea in the distance, I am reminded of a book called The Artist's Way, which extols simplicity and creativity through small, daily rituals. Seemingly simplistic, these daily routines that are (to my mind) linked to the pursuit of beauty, add other dimensions to the mundane aspects of life.

The Mother of Sri Aurobindo Ashram, who needs no introduction, has written a seminal work on the spiritual significance of flowers. It's a treatise that is both philosophical and artistic in its scope. Her samadhi shrine is adorned with flowers of incredible beauty. Matri Mandir is a structure of rare and pristine beauty. The meditation chamber offers a life-transforming experience to those who are open to it.

Gazing at the ocean from the seashore at Pondicherry, it strikes me that we, in the city, are increasingly removed from calm, a pre-requisite for creativity. A wise soul that I bump into at a little bookshop selling translations of books written in French, tells me that, "quietude, reflection, spontaneity...this is the way of the soul. We clutter the path with roadblocks in the form of unnecessary desires". Indeed.

The majority of Aurovillians live a creative life. It's a life sans chafing. Which is not to say they are not ambitious, successful, or in any way removed from the demands of the world and international trends. They have just learnt to tap into their intuitive selves and let their higher self guide them towards all that is necessary and required for a peaceful co-existence. Filled with reflections and age old discoveries, I am led to send a text to a friend who is aspiring to be an artist. It says, "If you want to learn form, study the shape of flowers." Eat, pray, love, to borrow from the title of a bestseller, is actually all that one needs to do.

(The columnist is a writer and a consultant)

Heading: Culture vulture - Indian Express
Content:
An important word that got overlooked a few columns ago while talking of Fluxus, and Pop Art was the 'found object'. Arthur Mendes, a fellow gallery trawler, once asked what exactly was the point and purpose of a found object and why was it called thus. To explain it the dictionary way, a found object is something that the artist or musician stumbles upon, but finds in it artistic possibilities.

Unlike objects that are created by the artist, a found object already exists for some other utilitarian purpose. Like Andy Warhol's Brillo boxes or Campbell soup cans. In the Indian context, artist Atul Dodiya often works with found objects, and places them in a cabinet, as a display. The object usually is a metaphor hinting at a meaning other than its literal one. For example, in the case of the Brillo boxes the objects were an entry point into a debate about consumerist, capitalist America.

Or in the case where Dodiya uses old bones and prosthetics he is referring to the state of the nation. Another famous example is Dadaist Marcel Duchamp's Fountain. The artist found a urinal, turned it upside down, signed it and called it art.

The found object can also function as a prop, almost like a Hitchcockian device that gives the viewer a clue. Like in the case of artist Sudarshan Shetty's installations. Found objects like old gramophones, a set of old scissors and an old bath tub, were assembled to make a macabre statement about the futility of entertainment.

In some cases, the object may hold a sentimental value and be displayed as an object of nostalgia, as when Himanshu Shetty used a collection of old school-books to talk about his childhood and make a larger statement on education of children. The point, however, of the found object is that it should be found and not looked for. In many instances, the search for these objects is too deliberate and it changes the nature of the 'found' status of the object.

(Demystify art, e-mail georgina.maddox@expressindia.com)

Heading: Sena man shot dead at Airoli - Indian Express
Content:
Lyrical colours
Musicians is a series of semi-abstract figurative paintings by artist Shakeel Momin; the artist uses watercolours on paper to create vibrant rhythmic overtures that at once portray serenity and joy. The figurative muse is that of Brahmin boys. The figures are engulfed with swirls of colour and have a mystical air about them.
At Gallery Pradarshak, Kalpana Building, Khar (West), till November 8

Sculpting dreams
Renowned Delhi-based, sculptor, Neeraj Gupta, is visiting the city to showcase his works at the city's popular gallery. Gupta's inspiration comes from nature. He extols the rock patters of stones found near the water's edge, heightens the textures and grain of wood in his work. Working with chisel and hammer, he uncovers figures, abstract forms and sometimes leaves the form as it is working with its natural charm.
At Jehangir Art Gallery, till November 6

Divine metaphor
Harish Kumar, a Faridabad based artist, is showcasing his paintings in an exhibition titled Mélange, at Art Entrance. Harish Kumar's paintings are really a mixture of richness in colours, thoughts, moods, sprit, divine love and tranquility. He uses images of Krishna, Lord Ganesha and Bhuddha in his painting as a metaphor for love, divinity and tranquility respectively. His paintings are not pure abstracts; they are executed in a stylistic figurative mode in which rhythmical line and texture plays major role.
At Art Entrace, Army & Navy Building, Kalaghoda, till November 7

Show all
ONE thing that will remain constant during the Prithvi Theatre Festival is their exhibition on Satyadev Dubey, called Theatre ke Anokhe Dubey. This is the third such exhibition on theatre personalities organised by the theatre hub in Juhu. This year's festival celebrates the contribution of Satyadev Dubey—his maverick madness, extreme generosity, and relentless work in theatre. The exhibition will be inaugurated on November 6 at 8 pm at Horniman Circle Garden.
At Horniman Circle Garden from 10 am-7 pm, November 7-16

Figures of speech

The artists have shown widely and are linked by their common love for figurative works. While Jaffar's surreal works look at the man woman dynamic, Tomar and Mujumdar are inspired by rustic life.

Heading: Metro Rail labourers among  scared migrants fleeing city - Indian Express
Content:
Officers of the Rabale police station are conducting inquiries to trace the identities and whereabouts of two men who are suspected to have shot Nitin Prabhu (27) on Saturday night. Prabhu was the Deputy Shakha Pramukh of the Shiv Sena office in Airoli, and also ran a real estate agency in the suburbs.

According to Rabale police, Nitin Prabhu was going to his office along with his friend Aniruddha Samant on the latter's motorbike, when Samant received a phone call on his cell phone.

"In order to speak on the phone, Samant pulled to the side of the road, just outside Asha Hospital in Sector 7. While he was talking, two unidentified men approached the duo on foot, fired three to four rounds and ran away," said DCP (Zone 1) RD Shinde. The duo then escaped on a motorbike, which they had parked some 50 to 60 feet away, he added.

While Prabhu received bullet injuries in the head and neck and died on the spot, Samant sustained an injury after a bullet grazed his neck and is currently recuperating in the Indravati Hospital in Sector 8 of Airoli.

An officer with the Rabale police said they suspect one Sanjay Jadhav, a former business partner of Prabhu to be involved in the incident. The two men had split paths after a disagreement a year ago and also had a big quarrel some 15 days ago, during which Jadhav had issued threats to Prabhu, the officer added.

Jadhav is currently absconding and the police are trying to trace him.

Heading: In far suburbs, railway accidents on rise along with population - Indian Express
Content:
Attacks by MNS coupled with Diwali-Chhat Puja season has caused scores of workers to return home

In a worrying fallout of the recent violence against North Indians in Mumbai combined with the festival season, scores of migrant labourers at Mumbai's first Metro Rail construction sites have left the city.

According to labourers at the construction site along the Right of Way of the Versova-Andheri-Ghatkopar corridor, the sense of insecurity among workers and a fear of further attacks and clashes looms large. "After his (Thackeray's) arrest many of us were worried about the situation we would face. Because of this fear, dozens of the daily wage labourers have fled to native places and have not returned since," said Shambhu Kumar, a labourer working at the construction site near Indian Oil Nagar, Andheri. Kumar, who originally hails from a village near Patna, added that on October 21 the labourers collected the day's wages and left to catch the first train back home.

Another labourer, Ram Parmesh, working on the Andheri-Kurla Road stretch also reiterated that many of the labourers had fled the construction sites.

Asked why he did not run away fearing attacks, Parmesh responded: "How can we run away? We can't afford it. What will we eat? And there is no point running away. These things happen and then things go back to normal in a few days."

Meanwhile, the spokesperson for the Mumbai Metro One Pvt Ltd declined to comment on the issue. "MMOPL and Simplex Infra, which has bagged the civil contract, would not want to comment on the issue of labourers," the spokesperson said. "Work has not been affected to a great extent, but we're hoping for the best. We, however, don't have a count of the number of labourers. That is the contractor's job...they will get more labourers from their other projects," said S C Gutpa, head of civil constructions for Mumbai Metro One Pvt Ltd.

Sources said the Reliance Infrastructure-led consortium is attempting to mobilise the labourers from other centres to come to Mumbai, not an easy task given the fear among labourers. "Another dampener for the MMOPL is that labourers have also gone back home for Diwali, apart from the fears of MNS-attacks, but it is not expected to delay the project in any way," said a source, requesting anonymity.

Heading: Compensation for families of Ghonse ghat bus tragedy - Indian Express
Content:
Increase in number of commuters not matched with adequate infrastructure, Rlys admit barricading not comprehensive

Alongside their swift growth, the satellite cities around Mumbai are also seeing a rise in the number of rail accidents.

According to figures obtained from the Mumbai railway police commissionerate, railway police stations at Vasai, Panvel and Vashi are seeing a steady increase in the number of deaths caused by railway accidents. Stations like Kalwa, Diva, Titwala, Kopar, Kalyan, Dombivli, Khaghar, Mansarovar and Panvel and stations beyond Kalyan have all witnessed a large growth in commutership, simultaneous to the rise in the population of these areas where realty has been more affordable. However, a simultaneous growth in infrastructure and services — even basic amenities like fencing and barricading — has been missing.

At Vasai railway police station, which has five railway stations under its jurisdiction from Mira Road to Virar, 2005 saw 278 accidental deaths, rising significantly to 290 in 2006 and 318 in 2007. The number till August this year is 173 accidental deaths.

The Vashi railway police station, which has in its jurisdiction all stations from Vashi to Belapur and from Airoli to Vashi on the harbour line has the same story to report. While accidental deaths were pegged at 142 in 2005, the number rose to 187 in 2006. In 2007, the figure was 182. Till August this year, 102 deaths were recorded by the Vashi railway police.

"These areas are seeing rapid urbanisation, but the infrastructure is very poor at these stations. All these stations need more foot overbridges (FOBs), barricading and blocking entry to prevent people from crossing tracks," said Aarti Bandgar ACP (Administration) of the Mumbai railway police who till the last week was holding charge of Vasai division. "We hold regular meetings with the railway to take measures in these cases."

Also, most accidental deaths in these areas are related to crossing tracks and falling down from running trains, a symptom of overcrowded commuter trains.

"We have track dividers on most of our stations. There are few stations (beyond Mira Road) which do not have these dividers, but we are working on it and we have plans to introduce these dividers on all our stations in order to deter people from crossing the tracks," said C Sharma, Divisional Railway Manager of the Western Railway. "Since last year, we have increased 78 services on the WR and all have been on the Virar section."

"Station areas beyond Vashi are seeing fast development in recent years, but the stations have been built by CIDCO," said Sriniwas Mudegrikar, chief spokesperson for Central Railway. "We would be having a meeting with the CIDCO officials to sort out this problem." The CR is also planning to start 12 car train services on the harbour line.

Heading: The Ringmaster Rules - Indian Express
Content:
A day after a Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC) bus plunged into Ghonse ghat near Raigad Tehsil killing 20 and injuring over 30 people, MSRTC has announced a compensation package of Rs 1 lakh for the families of those killed.

Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation Public Relations officer Mukund Dhus said, "Our chairman, Sudhakar Paricharak, has personally visited all the those recuperating in Sion hospital. He has also visited families whose members died in the unfortunate incident. We will take every measure to reach out to all the families." MSRTC has also taken up the responsibility of paying medical expenses of all the injured.

"We will take care of medical expenses worth Rs 1 lakh. If the amount goes beyond that we will verify the details and give the money," added Dhus.

MSRTC has also announced job opportunities to the family members of the driver and conductor of the bus who died in the accident.

Heading: Turbulence at Jet continues: Parts of pilots’ salaries ‘deferred’ - Indian Express
Content:
If a circus brings back memories of childhood, fire-eaters, clowns and the trapeze artistes, here's one you shouldn't miss

The spotlight lights up the circular stage, the nets are strung tight, the drum-rolls begin and as they reach a crescendo, a figure perched precariously on a ledge at the very top of the tent rubs his hands together and smiles confidently at the crowd below.

Suddenly, he jumps off the ledge and for one second, time stands still, as he remains suspended in air. While the crowd holds its breath and gasps collectively, the man reaches out and grabs a swinging bar.

The Trapeze Act has begun, and children and adults alike are gazing in awe and anticipation, for the Circus has come to town.

For those under the impression that an evening out at the circus has lost its charm, Rambo International Circus will prove otherwise. The 12-year-old circus has a new and improved look now, with an entirely air-conditioned interior and a hydraulic ring, something that is unique to them, since it is the only circus in India to have both amenities.

"We have three shows, at three o' clock, six o' clock and nine o'clock at night. The night show is almost always full, though there are crowds that turn up for the others too, they are fewer in numbers," says Mohan Shahani, who has been associated with the circus since its inception. "The circus was started by P T Dilip 12 years ago, in Pune in Saras Baug. He visited circuses all over the world and took the best example of their techniques and brought back technicians as well," he adds.

Rambo Circus is also the only one in India to have an ice-skating rink inside.

The Rambo International Circus lives up to its name, and has an array of artistes from around the world working with it. "We have men and women from Russia, New Zealand, Uzbekistan and Nepal, among other places like Maharashtra, Gujarat, Bengal and Kerala from within India," says Shahani. The circus has also won 21 gold medals in contests around the world

"We don't allow photography because the artistes get disturbed when they perform their acts. And we have acts lined up one after the other so that there is no time wasted between them," says Shahani. Altogether, there are 25 acts and many have fascinating, dramatic names — Boneless Acrobatics, Tarpaulin Dance, Dangerous Acrobatics, Russian Ball-Square Act, and the Spiderman Act, among others. The circus has finished a month in Ahmedabad and will be in Mumbai for the same duration before it moves on to set up camp in another city.

While tickets are priced anywhere between Rs 50 to Rs 200, the rotating ring helps everybody in the audience to catch a glimpse of some of the rich costumes and dramatic acts — huge elephants, an entertaining dog show and of course, the clowns.

As the comic capers begun, the little children in the crowd are laughing out loud, clapping their hands in glee. Whoever said that going to the circus isn't fun any more should spend an unusual evening out here.

Heading: Body found in bogie - Indian Express
Content:
Impending salary cuts at the country's largest private domestic carrier, Jet Airways, became crystal clear after 780 pilots and about a thousand engineering staff members received cuts in their salaries with October's pay. And, while the festive season lost its sheen for these employees, non-managerial staff members including Jet's cabin crew, their ground duty staff and others received Diwali bonuses along with their monthly remuneration.

To the pilots and engineering staffers, salary cuts came in the form of their retention bonus being cut. "I did get my salary this month but the retention bonus of Rs 20,000 that I get every month is not there," a Grade 5 aircraft maintenance engineer (AME) told Newsline. Engineering staff at Jet say that they are entitled to a retention bonus of Rs 1,20,000 every six months, which is paid in instalments of Rs 20,000 every month. "But this month it was missing," he said.

The pilots were not a happy lot either. "My co-pilot got only Rs 1,29,000 instead of the usual Rs 1,45,000," said a commandant who flies for Jet. "But cabin crew and others have even got a Diwali bonus with this month's salary," he added.

However, a Jet spokesperson said there were no salary cuts and that staff members had been told that part of their salaries had been deferred. "These are internal matters and we do not talk about it," the spokesperson said.

According to a source, all non-managerial staff at Jet received a Diwali bonus of Rs 8,400 and another Rs 1,000 as ex-gratia payment. A cabin crew staff member confirmed that they received the Diwali bonus along with their usual salaries.

An engineering staff-member said they had received an email from the company stating that their retention bonuses were being deferred due to the financial turbulence the company was facing. "We're watching the situation right now but if we don't get our full salaries then we'll decide what action to take," said a pilot.

A senior Jet official, on condition of anonymity, told this newspaper that eventually it's a question of demand and supply. "Now that we're curtailing flights, it's evident that there'll be more commanders and fewer planes to fly. Therefore, Jet will be in a position to dictate terms to them (pilots)," he said. Sources also confirmed that the airline will be grounding five Boeing 737-400 and two Boeing 737-NGs aircraft "You need a minimum of six sets of pilots per aircraft which directly puts 42 pilots on the bench apart from others who're already out there," said a pilot.

Heading: Rage for Robotics - Indian Express
Content:
The decomposed body of a 35-year-old unidentified person was found at the Lower Parel railway yard of Central Mumbai on Sunday. The police said that the body was found inside a bogie of a train.

"A Railway Protection Force (RPF) constable found the body in the afternoon while foot patrolling at the railway yard. The body was was emitting foul smell," the police said.

The constable then rushed to the Lower Parel railway station master who informed the N M Joshi Marg police station.

Considering the rotten state of the body, police suspect that it might have been lying inside the bogie for over a week. The body has been for post mortem.

Heading: Two die as car hits divider - Indian Express
Content:
At Tricks 2008, even a 12-year-old could take up robotics in an event conducted by The Robotics Institute

Unlike other kids his age, for 12-year-old Jay Gadre, Lego bricks were not just another toy. His first Lego kit, he recollects, got him hooked on to something he hopes to pursue as a career, robotics.

At Tricks 2008, a city-wide robotics competition conducted by The Robotics Institutes (TRI), this Jamnabai Narsee student battled it out with over 150 students from 36 schools in Mumbai at the Indian Institute of technology campus at Powai on Sunday. TRI is a venture by a group of Indian Institute of Technology Bombay (IITB) alumni.

Gadre, the youngest of all the participants, won the competition meant for 14-18 year olds, along with his partner and classmate Soham Bhatnagar.

The competition was held to test the 'robotic skills' of the students through autonomous and on-the-spot competitions. "The participants were given problem statements for building autonomous robots, capable of identifying victims whilst navigating over a line on the floor and also in the absence of the line. The robot should also be able to navigate through debris and climb a ramp," explained Varun Jain, media coordinator of TRI.

In order to acquaint students with the basics of robotics before the competition, TRI conducted free robotic workshops called Fundae sessions in various places in Mumbai in September and October which saw participation of over 500 students from around 75 schools.

Operating under the brand name of ThinkLABS and robo.in, Powai-based TRI has been in the business of robotics education for over two-and-a-half years. TRI intends to work closely with school systems to reach students by means of interactive communication channels and to work with teachers and students on robotic research, added Jain. ThinkLABS is one of the companies incubated by IIT Bombay's Society for Innovation and Entrepreneurship (SINE).

Gagan Goyal, director of TRI, said, "TRI believes that an early association with robotics will help forge a lifelong attachment to science and technology and this is the goal that TRICKS aims to achieve by making young minds to join the league which will lead the country towards a technical revolution."

Another participant, Jehaan Nicholson, 14, of Ashok Academy, Andheri, who finished his task in an impressive three minutes, said: "The workshops helped me immensely. I had seen similar competitions at Techfest (IIT's science and technology festival) and seen similar competitions. I would like to take up engineering and specialise in robotics."

Heading: City to celebrate 66 years of association with St Petersburg - Indian Express
Content:
Two persons were killed and another two injured in Borivali when a speeding Hyundai Accent hit the divider on Link Road around 7:30 on Sunday morning.

The driver, a businessman named Pravin Bhatt, has been arrested on charges of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, rash driving and causing grievous hurt and endangering life. Bhatt has been remanded to judicial custody for seven days.

According to police, at the time the incident occurred a crowd had gathered outside a mobile toilet stationed at the Ganpat Patil Road near the Link Road leading to Dahisar.

"The driver has given a statement that he was trying to control his vehicle and save another pedestrian who was crossing the road," said Senior Police Inspector Krushnaji Gaikwad. He added, "That is when the car hit the divider and then hit the people who had gathered to use the loo. Two of them were squatting on the road itself."

The two deceased have been identified as Premshankar Mishra (35) and Sanju Kapar (25), and the two injured in the accident are Ramnarayan Vishwakarma (25) and Vinod Shankar (35). The bodies of the deceased were taken to Bhagwati Hospital for postmortem. The medical report of Pravin Bhatt is still awaited.

Heading: Robbery at Nalasopara jewellery store - Indian Express
Content:
In A unique celebration of completing 66 years of cultural exchanges with St Petersburg, the otherwise fuddy-duddy Brihanumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) is all set to host a series of colourful events from Russian painting exhibitions to ballets.

As it completes 66 years of the "sister-city relationship" with St Petersburg, Mumbai can look forward to Russian ballet performances, a Russian opera and an exhibition of exquisite Russian oil paintings in a three-day event from November 5 to 7.

The sister-city programme is a unique facilitation for a cultural exchange, to give countries a sneak peek into different cultures. Earlier this year, in February, Mumbai celebrated 40 years of the sister-city relationship with Stuttgart.

St.Petersburg, located in North-West Russia on the Baltic Sea, is often described as the most Western-style city of Russia. Known for its rich culture, the city is home to some famous artistes, ballet dancers and singers.

The St Petersburg sister-city committee regularly organizes Russian-themed cultural events like film festivals, world class ballets, art exhibitions and musical evenings with some the Russia's most established and emerging musical artistes. This year, famous Russian names like Irina Birulya, an award winning stage designer and painter and opera singers from the Mariinsky theatre opera group will be seen showcasing their talents among others, at the National Centre for Performing Arts, Nariman Point.

"We welcome all kind of sister-city programmes. Such initiatives open up a new door to learn more about an alien culture. Apart from that it also fosters interaction of different global communities. Further we can develop this relationship and get help for any kind of developmental work," said Mumbai Mayor Shubha Raul. At present, Mumbai shares a sister-city relationship with cities in 16 countries.

The official delegation from St Petersburg is scheduled to arrive on November 4. "The official delegation will be headed by Russian deputy governor Alexander Vakhmistrov," said Municipal Commissioner Jairaj Phatak.

Heading: When a motorman went up a mountain - Indian Express
Content:
The Nalasopara police are on the lookout for two men in their early twenties for their involvement in the robbery of jewellery worth Rs. 16 lakh from a jewellery shop in Nalasopara on Saturday night. According to police, the robbers used diwali crackers for creating confusion and making their getaway.

According to Senior Police Inspector of Nalasopara police station Sharad Ugale, "The shop, Swati Jewellery, located at the 18th Road in the ground floor of the New Sagar building was open on Saturday night at 8:15 when the incident took place. The owner, Ramesh Bohra (46) was in the shop with his son, Vedant (19) and some other staff members were helping customers with their purchases when the incident took place."

As per the statements given by Bohra and his son, a man rushed into the shop armed with a chopper and tried to attack Bohra. Bohra ducked under the counter and pressed the alarm button while dodging the blow.

"As soon as the alarm sounded, another man rushed in and threw diwali crackers called 'aapti bombs' in the shop. These are the kind of crackers, which burst on impact, creating smoke and loud noise. The sounds and smoke disoriented the customers and the owner, while the second man, who had thrown the crackers snatched the jewellery from the display counters and fled away with the armed man," said Ugale.

Though police from a nearby chowky reached the spot within minutes, the crowd made it impossible for the cops to apprehend the robbers. "We believe that the men must have left Nalasopara by train as after the incident, we created road blocks on all exits but could not catch them. We are preparing their sketches for identification," said Ugale.

Heading: Tamasha Mahotsav from today - Indian Express
Content:
What this amateur photographer brought down from every mountaineering expedition were startlingly beautiful images of snow in various forms

Munesh Kulshrestha is a motorman whose daily job keeps him rooted to Mumbai and its lifeline, the suburban railways, always buzzing with activity and always crowded. Kulshrestha's heart beats for Mumbai city, he says, but his dreams are elsewhere — higher, calmer and literally, snow white.

Last fortnight, his dreams found expression of photographs by the simple motorman — titled 'Himpressions', his photographs were on display at the National Centre for the Performing Arts from October 15 to 24.

The photographs were all shot by the amateur photographer on his Canon S2 digital and on his Nikon F-2 during the various expeditions in the Himalayas — his impressions of 'him', or snow. That's why, the exhibition featured artistic impressions of snow in all its forms, crystals, icicles, glaciers and mountain-tops.

Munesh, a well-known mountaineer of Western Railway, has been serving as a motorman for the past 20 years.

"Since childhood, I loved to click photographs but as it was a costly affair, I began to spend on this hobby only after I got a job," he says.

As a hobby turned into a passion, Munesh worked on his technique, sharpening the skills required to operate a camera at high altitudes.

Having joined the railways in 1988 as a motorman, and having been an avid mountaineer in college through the NCC, he has escaped on treks and mountaineering expeditions during every holiday he took. Encouraged by a photographer and mountaineer friend, he moved from using an SLR Zenith to the NIKON F-2, the Canon A-1 and digital Canon S2 IS.

"There are always unusual things in the mountains. I clicked a photograph of a river near Sonmarg while returning to the Amarnath cave. This river's shape resembled a duck, so I titled it a Riverbird Paradise," Munesh saus.

Several of his photographs show a combination of dark blue sky and clouds in different shapes; a picture of a full moon with snow snowfall and star trails surrounding it is also among his favourites.

Also founder-member of Western Railway's Adventure Sports Association and Rail Aarogya Yog Sanstha, Munesh has been to Mt Baljuri, Mt CB-54 in 1997, Mt Stok Kangri in 2001. He was deputy leader of an expedition to Mt Jogin - I & III in 2002 and the leader of an expedition to Avalanche Peak & Mt Kalindi in 2003. He also was a liaison officer with foreign teams — scaling Mt Shivling in1998 with a German team, a French team for Mt Shivling in 2000, Mt Stok Kangri in 2001 with a Spanish team, Mt Lungser Kangri in 2005 with a Japanese team and Mt Nun in 2007 with an Italian team. From the Valley to ladakh, from Amarnath to the Nilgiris and from the Valley of Flowers to Gangotri-Badrinath, Munesh has photographic memories of each spot.

The silence of the mountains and nature's bounties are what draws him to undertake arduous climbs. While his photographs have been displayed at different photo galleries as well as by the Photographic Society of India, his latest exhibition of photographs at the NCPA is his biggest exhibition till date.

Apart from demonstrating various emotions, feelings and colours of ice in its natural shades, these photographs also lead you to an echo, if you look, and listen carefully. q

Heading: Rs 85-lakh jewellery heist at Khar - Indian Express
Content:
In a bid to promote 'Tamasha' — one of the oldest forms of folk art in Maharashtra — the Maharashtra cultural department along with City and Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra (CIDCO) have planned a week long festival titled 'Maharashtra Dholki Fad Tamasha Mahotsav' at Navi Mumbai from Monday.

CIDCO chief Nakul Patil and Vidhan Parishad member Medha Mhatre will inaugurate the event. Participants from across Maharashtra— including Nashik, Jalgaon, Ahemadnagar, Dhule, Sangli and Narayangaon— will come together to perform in the seven-day festival.

Tamasha, often a naughty form of expression replete with double entendres and light-hearted story-telling by female artistes, has been on the decline over the last few years.

Haribhai Bade Nagarkar, one of the veterans in this art form, will be awarded at the CDICO Tamasha Mahotsav. Alongside some monetary support, the CIDCO plans to award him a memento for his enormous contribution towards keeping alive the folk art form.

Last year too, CIDCO, along with Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation, had organised a similar event to preserve the dying art, and got phenomenal response. This year's festival is to be held at the grounds opposite Vashi railway station.

Heading: Flyover plan forces traffic diversion - Indian Express
Content:
A gang of four robbers looted cash and jewellery worth approximately Rs 85 lakh from a jewellery shop located in Khar on Sunday morning.

The shop- Dinesh Jewellers- is in the Khardanda area in Khar and according to the Khar police where a case of robbery has been registered, it is usually closed on Sundays. Senior police inspector Ajit Sawant from the Khar police station said, "However, on some Sundays, the shop is open in the morning for some time and this was the time when the robbery took place." As per the statement given by the owner of the shop, Pankaj Jagawat, the robbery took place at 10 am. At the time of the incident Pankaj and his nephew were inside the shop and there was a security guard as well. "The security guard had gone to fill his bottle when two men, posing as customers, entered the shop. While we were dealing with them, the two other men also barged into the shop with guns and threatened us," said Jagawat. After immobilizing them, the four snatched the keys to the lockers where the jewellery was stored and fled with cash and jewellery worth an approximate value of Rs 85 lakh.

"The men were in the age group of 38-40 years and were dressed reasonably well. With their short sleeved shirts and haircuts, we initially thought of them as police officials before they started pulling out guns. As our security guard is not provided with a weapon, he was helpless," said Jagawat. He added that the shop is not equipped with CCTV cameras.

"Based on the description provided by Jagawat, we are drawing sketches of the four men and shall be circulating them so as to narrow down on them and identify the robbers," said Sawant.

Heading: Thane’s water woes set to end by March - Indian Express
Content:
With construction of a flyover set to start soon at the Datta Mandir Sainath Subway Junction of Western Express Highway at Kurar Village, the traffic authorities and the Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation (MSRDC) have decided to implement a set of traffic restrictions owing to the large volume of traffic at theplace. The flyover is being constructed under the Mumbai Urban Infrastructure Project. The changes in the traffic routes, for smooth flow of traffic and for overall safety at the construction site, are as follows:

* For the traffic coming from Samtanagar Kandivali near Times of India and going to Datta Mandir Road for Sainath Subway, right turn is closed .

* For going to Malad (East), traffic will go further on WEH upto Pathanwadi / Ranisati Subway, take a 'U' turn under this subway and go to Malad (East) via Daftary Road & Rani Sati Marg.

* For going to Malad (West), traffic will go further on WEH upto Dindoshi Flyover take a right turn under the flyover, go to Goregaon Mulund Link road and reach Malad (West) via Pravasi Junction, Pandurangwadi and Savarkar Bridge.

* For traffic coming from Mamaledar wadi and going to Datta Mandir road via Sainath Subway left turn is closed . Vehicles will have to take a right turn after crossing the subway, take a left turn at Malad (East) railway station chowk and go to Daftary Road or Pushpa Park (Shantaram Talav) via Ranisati Marg or Pathanwadi/ Ranisati Subway via Ranisati Marg.

* Traffic will be allowed to take right / left turn at Ranisati subway location to go WEH.

* For the traffic on WEH coming from Goregaon side to Kandivali side and going to Datta Mandir Road, left turn will remain available .  

* The left turn remains available for local traffic coming from Datta Mandir Road to go to WEH south side via right turn under Akurli Subway or via right turn under Thakur Complex Junction.

Heading: Soon, conservancy staff to get permanent homes - Indian Express
Content:
Residents of the rapidly growing Thane city will soon find their daily struggle for water coming to an end. For, newly developed upscale residential constructions in the city adjoining the financial capital as well as several sprawling slum pockets are set to benefit from the early completion of the Thane Municipal Corporation's ambitious 110 million litres a day (mld) water supply scheme, now set to be commissioned in March 2009.

The project has been completed a year ahead of the official deadline.

Thane city's water woes have been so severe that a few months ago, the corporation had appealed to the neighboring Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation no provide about 40 mld of water to enhance the supply to the city's 17-lakh strong population. Some areas received civic water supply only once in 36 hours.

"All the work on the scheme is complete. We have already started lifting water partly. Full water supply form this project will begin in March," said city engineer of the Thane Municipal Corporation (TMC) K D Lala.

As many as 7 lakh people are expected to benefit from the 110 mld water scheme.

The biggest area to benefit will be Ghodbunder Road, home to scores of large housing complexes and a seemingly endless array of new construction sites. The hilly region of Wagle estate and the slum areas of Indira Nagar will also benefit.

While water connections in many of these areas was partly through the MIDC, the TMC will now be able to supply water on its own in these regions.

At a cost of Rs 72 crore, the project was constructed under the Centre's Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) and involved laying of additional water pipelines, modifying the existing pumping station and augmenting the filtration plant at Temghar, in order to lift water from a weir at Bhatsa and in the Pise region.

The existing water supply of Thane city is 390 mld, set to rise to 500 mld with the addition of this project. The new scheme will be able to fulfill the water supply needs for an estimated population of 22 lakh till 2016, it is estimated.

Thane city has witnessed a growth of six-seven per cent per annum. "In the last few years, Ghodbunder Road has developed rapidly with a number of high-rises and housing complexes. The hilly areas on the northern side of Thane were also deprived of adequate water. Now all these places will get sufficient water," he added. "We could neither stop development or tell builders to go slow on construction. Upgradation of the existing infrastructure was most necessary."

Heading: Inner Circle - Indian Express
Content:
* A dream comes true for 90,000 workers across Maharashtra
* Of 27,000 workers in Mumbai, only 5,000 have quarters

When liver malfunction claimed his father's life three years ago, Nitin Jogadia was an average student who did a fine balancing act with his studies at the reputed Sydenham College and his part time job as a sales executive.

But fate had different plans for Nitin who today works as a BMC sweeper like his late father did for 25 years of his life. "With two younger brothers who were still studying, I had no choice but to take up my father's job as a civic sweeper if I wanted to retain the roof over our head," said the commerce graduate who still cherishes his dreams for a good career but believes that he 'acted responsibly' by giving up his respectable job and salary for the sake of his family.

As in the case of Nitin, growing literacy rates in the community have failed to liberate families of conservancy workers from the hold of their traditional occupation. Generations after generation are forced to choose the broom over the pen in a bid to retain the limited quarters allotted to their deceased parents or husbands.

In a policy decision that would chart out a different future for children of the 90,000 civic conservancy workers across Maharashtra, the state government has decided to make it mandatory for all municipal corporations and councils to provide permanent homes to conservancy workers who have completed over 25 years in service or to the close relatives of workers who die while in service.

In a recent notification issued by the Urban Development department, the government has said that it would reserve 15 per cent of houses in existing projects — such Low Income Group housing, Integrated Housing and Slums Development Programme (IHSDP), Basic Services to the Urban Poor (BSUP) and surplus flats generated under the Slum Rehabilitation Scheme — for conservancy workers' housing.

It also states that if the civic body decides to implement a mass housing project for such workers on its land or on land owned by state government, then the project will be granted a maximum Floor Space Index (FSI) of 4. If the same project is carried out through a private builder, he will be allowed 50 per cent of the total built up area as his incentive FSI.

Presently, there is an acute shortage of quarters for these workers which had made permanent homes a distant dream. In Mumbai itself, of the 27,000 workers barely 5,000 are lucky enough to live in quarters.

"Our proposed scheme, which will increase the stock of both quarters and permanent homes, aims at improving the lot of workers in solid waste management department. Considering that about 4 per cent of these workers retire every year in the state, we will have to generate around 4000 homes annually," said Urban Development secretary Manu Kumar Srivastava.

All local bodies will be required to reserve 5 per cent of their budgetary provision for the weaker section each year for the purpose of constructing houses for conservancy workers. The state government will also release funds for such projects as and when required.

Heading: A new cut - Indian Express
Content:
Two top-lining model and fashion designer deconstruct Madhur Bhandarkar's Fashion

In his movie Fashion that released this week, Madhur Bhandarkar plays himself in a cameo. The frame catches him sitting in the front row of a fashion show, while characters whisper in awestruck tones that he is there researching his latest project—the fashion industry. This self-congratulatory pat on his back is possibly the least irksome part of Bhandarkar's three-hour-fifteen-minute-long movie. Watching it in PVR, model Sonalika Sahay and designer

Vineet Bahl protest vehemently about the movie and Bhandarkar, who has built a reputation as a hard-hitting filmmaker doesn't dumb down to appease the audience.

"It is very clichéd. He has strung together a few sensational events and tried to filter an opinion through them," says Sahay. Sahay's ire is directed at the screenplay of the movie—the story of three models: a small-town beauty pageant winner, played by Priyanka Chopra, who makes it big very fast, a supermodel played by Kangana Ranaut who is addicted to drugs and alcohol and a second-rung model, Mugdha Godse, who figures out how to hold her own in the big, bad world of modelling. Bhandarkar's disclaimer at the beginning of the movie that all the characters and events are fictitious doesn't ring true as a doped-out Ranaut lands up on the footpath a la Gitanjali Nagpal, and Chopra's character descends into the allegedly murky side of fashion —dope, alcohol and rehab, much like England-educated Shivani Kapur did a couple of years back.

"Bhandarkar should have given the movie a broader perspective. This whole thing about small-town girls losing their heads in modelling is so insulting. I'm from Bihar and let me tell you, exploitation is a matter of choice," says Sahay. "There's a nicer side to the industry as well, like friendships and creativity."

The stress on supermodels and showstoppers throughout the movie, says Sahay, is also dated. "It's something that used to happen in the initial stages of the industry. We are way past those days when a show was only about the showstopper. The only believable bit about the movie is Mugdha, probably because being part of the industry, she knows how it works and makes it look a little more credible," she says.

Designer Vineet Bahl agrees in part with Sahay. While he is impressed with the histrionics of Chopra and Ranaut, his grouse is about the male characters, most of whom have been stereotyped as gay designers and exploitative agency owners. "Bhandarkar could have done without gross generalisations. It makes the movie shallow and over-dramatic. Also, there is nothing about the clothes. Whatever they show on the ramp in the movie is extremely amateurish, straight out of some fashion student's costume fantasy," says Bahl. "What is credible about the movie is the rise and fall of the two lead characters — Priyanka and Kangana. Their attempt to hold onto 15 minutes of fame is something you see in the industry all the time," he says.

Heading: I Quit - Indian Express
Content:
Manasi Joshi Roy now takes the director's seat

After Manasi Joshi Roy, the actor turned producer, she insisted on adding 'creative' as suffix to her new role. "I always believe that I'm a creative producer, and not just a producer. I like designing my complete show which I'm doing with Cinemascope", says Joshi.

Joshi Roy's prowess as a director will come to the fore today when Zee Muzic launches a new season of Cinemascope. The Bollywood-based show hosted by Roshni Chopra will take the viewers through new releases and their making, besides filling them in with all the gossip related to the films and its cast. It will also package reviews, previews and the box-office outcomes. The small screen might experience a surfeit of such programmes but the newly-turned director claims that her show, replete with trivia will stand out. "Apart from trivia, interviews with actors and behind-the-scene footage are going to be our USPs," she says.

Though direction is very fulfilling, Joshi Roy doesn't want to take up more such assignments right now. After setting the template of Cinemascope and directing its initial episodes, her focus will shift to acting—which remains her abiding passion. Production will also take up her time. She has launched a production house, called Magic Works, with husband Rohit Roy. Both of them are involved in its creative processes while administration remains Joshi Roy's domain.

However, the actor, who won hearts as Sudha in Saaya, has no plans of appearing on the small screen any time soon. "Not until I get something exciting," she says. Next summer, she will appear on the big screen when Alibaug releases. The year 2009 will also see the release of Pankh, which is co-produced by the Roys. "We are very happy to have made a non-mainstream film like Pankh. We want to produce more films in future. At present, however, we don't have anything exciting to talk about," she says.

After mapping a successful journey in the world of entertainment, the actor, who has her roots in theatre, longs to go back to stage. "I wish to do some plays sometime soon," says the daughter of Arvind Joshi, an eminent Gujarati theatre personality.

Heading: Chatterati - Indian Express
Content:
Shankar Mahadevan and Ustad Rashid Khan prove they're in tune with each other

Classical and pop music sensation Shankar Mahadevan and Hindustani classical maestro Ustad Rashid Khan have shared the stage before. But that was many years ago on the shores of Benares, along with other renowned artistes. And ever since, many fans have hoped that the two artistes would take the stage together once again. Thanks to the efforts of Shashi Vyas of Pancham Nishad, Mumbai will witnessed their union on Sunday. Being touted as a "first time ever unique jugalbandi", Samanvay will be a programme to watch for several reasons.

Indian classical music's history has had a tradition of unforgettable jugalbandis, with the likes of Ravi Shankar with Ustad Ali Akbar Khan and Bhimsen Joshi with Dr Balamuralikrishna.

This concert was especially interesting to music lovers as it was the coming together of a singer trained in the Hindustani classical tradition (Rashid Khan) and another in a Carnatic school (Mahadevan). So how did the two artists from such diverse musical styles decide to join hands?

Mahadevan, who has been actively involved with the Hindi cinema music scene —with recent chart toppers like the Rock On soundtrack — says: "It is our mutual appreciation and admiration for each other's work that brings us together to begin with. The idea was to share a space and explore what will happen. It is also an attempt to expand our own horizons and styles."

Khan, who has emerged as one of the most promising names in the younger generation of Hindustani singers, comes from the Sahaswan Gharana. He has had a long association with the Sangeet Research Academy in Kolkata, which he quit in 1999 to found his own academy.

Today, he is something of legend in classical music circles, poised to rise to the stature of greats like Bhimsen Joshi and Kumar Gandharva. The artists are quick to clarify the purist nature of the concert. "It is not a fusion concert, but a classical bandish" says Mahadevan.

The notion that there are no takers amongst the youth for classical music may also be changing as more and more independent musicians in the country display strong strains of classical influence.

And Khan is happy to join hands with Mahadevan to promote the art. "The kala is the most important thing. Such concerts are an effort in the right direction because the new generation will get to listen to music they normally might not listen to."

Heading: Modi upsets Gupta, in lead - Indian Express
Content:
Hollywood nights
In a small and close media gathering, Sony Pix unveiled its new show, Chicks on Flicks, on Friday at the Four Seasons Hotel. With Ira Dubey and Neha Sareen as reviewers, the show will critique Hollywood flicks that release in theatre or on DVD in India.
The event saw a weak attendance but business head Sunder Aaron kept his audience entertained. Neha's opening lines sounded like a rehearsed speech as she went on to 'share' her emotions over being selected as a reviewer for the show. The girls, eager to prove their mettle, shared their views on a host of films.
Showstopper Sunder's good looks, intellect and charm beat the girls and anchored the get-together.

Boo!
In their first ever public appearance, cast of Raaz - The Mystery Continues attended the Halloween party at Hard Rock Café on Friday. Keeping in spirit of the celebration, Emraan Hashmi and Adhyayan Suman, along with director Mohit Suri, unveiled the Raaz promos. Other guests included Tarana Raj Kapoor and Nina Manuel.
The famous serial-kisser realised that he has an equally besotted male fan following when a masked guy began to haunt him and refused to budge unless he had his photograph clicked with the actor. Disarmingly, Emraan obliged.
Bummer It was a Halloween party but none of the stars, dressed in casual tees, looked the part.

Heading: Satguru raiders shock BSNL - Indian Express
Content:
Kunal Modi (ELO 1722) outwitted the sole leader Atit Gupta (ELO 1726) in the under-17 boys group of Mumbai Youth Interschool Chess Championship, organised by the Venus Chess Academy, hosted by the Goregaon Sports Club and conducted by the Bombay Chess Association.

In the sixth round and penultimate round, seventh seed Kunal Modi of Thakur Vidya Mandir Kandivali was playing with white pieces against fifth seed Atit Gupta of St. Lawrence School, Borivali. Using the Yugoslav attack against Atit's dragon in Sicilian defence, Kunal castled in the queen's wing while Atit castled in the king's wing. Kunal opened h and g files by exchanging pawns in front of black king and harassed the black king. In a hopeless position, Atit accepted his defeat in 35 moves. Kunal, Atit and third seed Amit Sukhpal (ELO 1883) jointly lead the field with 5 points each after the sixth round.

Amit of KVIIT Powai, playing with black pieces won on time with more or less equal position against Suraj Borate(ELO 1828) of Fr. Agnel, Vashi. Top seed Shantanu Bhambure(ELO 1945) drew with Karefegar Dalal and is in joint second spot with 4.5 points along with Bhaumik Doshi of Somaiya College, Vidyavihar who defeated Haresh Chodnekar.

In the U-17 girls group after sixth round, top seed Shilpi Jain of N M College defeated Priyanka Bahule and emerged sole leader with 5.5 points, while third seed Filisha Shah of AVM Juhu is alone in the second spot with 5 points after beating Anmol Soni. Second seed Bhakti Juikar(ELO 1768) of VN Sule Dadar is trailing behind on third spot with 4.5 points. She beat Priya Lotlikar of St. Ann's High School Borivali.

At the end of the fifth round in the U-11 boys group, Tejas Patkar of Fr. Angel, Vashi and Shreyas Kulakarni of Gokuldham, Goregaon are jointly leading the group with 5 points each. Both of them have won all five games in a row.

Top seed Sairaj Chittal of Balmohan Vidya Mandir was held to a draw by Vaibhav Bhat . Sairaj (ELO 1860), Vaibhav, and second seed Anand Prabhu are on jointly second spot with 4.5 points each. Anand Prabhu with black pieces defeated Arnav Desai of Greenlawns, Worli.

In the under-11 girls group at the end of fifth round, Vrushali Deodhar of Parle Tilak Vidyalaya is leading the field with 5 points. Vrushali who outwitted Devika Kelkar in the 5th round has won all the five games in a row.

Top seed Parnali Dharia (ELO 1634) of Madhavrao Bhagwat High School Vile Parle and third seed Janhavi Soneji( ELO 1476) of Cannossa Convent Andheri are jointly on the second spot. With 4 points each. Parnali was held to draw by second seed Dhanashree Pandit (ELO 1562) of NES, Bhandup, while Janhavi with black pieces defeated Shubhada Sawant of KES School, Santacruz.
