In the scenario of the BJD winning about 70 seats, Naveen can form a government minus the BJP with a little help from some independents. It could prove politically suicidal for us," said a senior BJP leader.

The Chief Minister who has been at the receiving end of the diatribe by the VHP and the Bajrang Dal for showing "undue sympathy" to Christians told a TV channel that the Bajrang Dal was a fundamentalist organisation.

Naveen also caught the BJP off-guard after he started his electoral campaign from tribal-dominated Koraput district all alone. Quick to realise Naveen's strategy of trying to keep his secular image intact in the aftermath of Kandhamal riots, the party is now going all out to put pressure on the Government to strictly enforce the provisions of the Orissa Freedom of Religion Act and Orissa Cow-Slaughter Prohibition Act, both of which were passed at least four decades ago, but have hardly been invoked.

Several BJP leaders say that the party has to continue with its aggressive stance over Kandhamal and highlight the ordeal of Kondh tribals at the hands of the CRPF and Orissa police, while keeping the issue of the murder of Laxmanananda alive in the minds of Hindu voters. "Despite what the Government claims, the regular gherao of police stations in Kandhamal by aggrieved tribal women shows that not everything is fine. The tribals are still angry," said a BJP MP.

In spite of its attempts to whip up public sentiments over Kandhamal, the BJP is not sure of its impact. Though the Sangh Parivar is well-networked in the state through its subsidiary organisations like the Vishwa Hindu Parishad and Vanavasi Kalyan Ashrams, the BJP ministers have zero credibility among the people as well as the cadres as the party.

Despite all his failings and lack of administrative abilities, Naveen has a far better image than any BJP leader of Orissa, which the party finding hard to ignore.

Heading: Migrants issue makes NCP, Cong redraw poll strategies in Maha - Indian Express
Content:
After the sixth Pay Commission nearly doubled the Travelling Allowance (TA) of senior officers, the government says it won't make additional funds available for the increased expenditure. It wants officers to cut official travel drastically to neutralize the effect of the increased TA.

In the time of global financial crisis, the government's latest memorandum on austerity measures reminds officers that "the new Travelling Allowance rules clearly state that no additional funds will be provided on account of revision of TA/DA entitlements". Officers should, therefore, travel "judiciously", "restricted only to absolutely essential officials requirements".

In June, the government had asked all ministries and departments to mandatorily cut 10 per cent cut of their non-plan expenditure.

The new memorandum, issued by the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance, asks each ministry or department to ensure that airline discounts are utilized in the best manner for the benefit of the government, and the cheapest tickets should be bought, "preferably by getting information through the Internet".

"Officers," it adds, "may also be encouraged, although not mandated, to travel by a class lower than their entitlements."

They are required to credit air miles accumulated on official travel to their departments, not to their personal accounts.

"Any other incentives and similar packages such has 'free companion' etc. should be so negotiated by the Ministries/ Departments so that the benefits come to the government," the memorandum says.

Officers have been advised to stay in circuit houses, government guest houses, inspection bungalows etc, while on tour.

Heading: Cong caught between RJD and NCP - Indian Express
Content:
Jittery after the polarisation of north Indian politicians against Maharashtra over the recent incidents against migrants in the state, the ruling partners of the Democratic Front Government — the Congress and the NCP — are working on fresh strategies in the run-up to the Lok Sabha and Assembly polls.

The NCP is planning to parade north Indian members of the party in front of the media, asking them to speak out against leaders like Lalu Prasad Yadav, Ram Vilas Paswan, Sharad Yadav and Mayawati on the issue of migrants being under threat of harm in Maharashtra. It also intends to rope in senior leaders like Tariq Anwar, D P Tripathi and north Indian leaders from Maharashtra to speak out in favour of Maharashtra in order to consolidate the party's position among migrants.

The Congress, on the other hand, will centre its campaign on advocating peace and harmony among different sections of society.

"The idea is to make our leaders hailing from states like Uttar Pradesh and Bihar to endorse that all citizens, including north Indian migrants, are safe in Maharashtra and that what is appearing in the media is highly exaggerated," general secretary of the Maharashtra unit of the NCP Gurunath Kulkarni said. "Maharashtra has a history of being a progressive state and has been tolerant of migrants. The impression created by media by telecasting one or two incidents repeatedly throughout the day does not mean that law and order has broken down."

He further said that preference to locals in jobs was not a new issue discovered by the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS), but was a policy of the state Government for years. He added that anyone residing in the state for more than 15 years was considered a 'local' person irrespective of whether he was born in Maharashtra or Bihar.

The NCP appears to be facing the flak more than the Congress, as Deputy Chief Minister R R Patil (NCP) holds the home portfolio and is blamed for any law and order problem. Moreover, Patil's justification of the death of Rahul Raj (the gun-toting youth in a Mumbai bus) in a police encounter and his outburst — "bullet for a bullet" — has landed the party in further trouble.

Meanwhile, the Congress is planning to involve eminent personalities from various fields to participate in its 'peace and harmony' campaign. "Our party has always risen above parochial issues and canvassed for votes on the issue of development," the president of the Maharashtra Pradesh Congress Committee Manikrao Thakre said. "And development is possible only if there is peace...we'll change the vitiated atmosphere."

A senior Congress functionary, however said, "With the MNS and Shiv Sena raking up issues of concern to local people, we are sandwiched between Marathis and north Indians. Our workers are asking what our Union ministers are doing for the Marathi cause, while north Indians are saying that we are soft on Raj Thackeray."

Beginning with Nashik on November 5 and 6, the Congress is planning to hold training workshops for its cadres "to enable them to reach out to the masses with the party's correct policies."

Besides, Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh and NCP chief Sharad Pawar are to launch a 'Bharat Jodo' campaign on November 14 in Mumbai to enhance the secular image of their parties.

Heading: J-K govt launches ad blitz urging people to vote - Indian Express
Content:
Caught between pressure from its allies from Bihar and political expediency with regard to Maharashtra, which is ruled by it, the Congress on Monday did a tightrope walk. In an apparent bid to take a high moral ground over the politics of oneupmanship in Bihar with its ally RJD and the latter's rival in the state JD(U) threatening that their members would resign from the Lok Sabha if action is not taken against MNS chief Raj Thackeray, the Congress accused the JD(U) of "political opportunism" and at the same time endorsing Lalu Prasad's proposal of a joint action.

The party, however, also defended the son-of-the-soil policy as echoed by its Maharashtra ally NCP but said violence against north Indians could not be allowed. Congress' balancing act came a day after NCP leader and Union Minister Praful Patel echoed the need for maintaining a "Maharashtrian ethos" in an interview on CNN-IBN's Devil's Advocate programme.

NCP chief Sharad Pawar, on the other hand, has chosen to keep to himself on the issue. "Everything is fabricated.... This is irresponsible....I have seen the reports....I just don't want to talk to the media," Pawar is learnt to have remarked to reporters over exaggerated politicisation of what he termed as "blown-out-of-proportion violence against north Indians" and added that he was "not a leader of one state".

"We have proposed that all MPs and MLAs of Bihar resign to project a united face on the issue. Why only Lok Sabha MPs, why not Rajya Sabha MPs and members of both Houses of the state legislature. However, the JD(U) offered that only its MPs would resign when the tenure of the Lok Sabha is just a couple of months away," Congress spokesperson Shakeel Ahmed said endorsing the Railway Minister's stand.

Heading: Wanted: candidates for Janata Party - Indian Express
Content:
The battle to conduct elections in Jammu and Kashmir is now being fought on a different terrain - in the pages of local newspapers in the state. To counter the separatist poll boycott call, the state government has launched an ad campaign in the local newspapers to persuade people to vote.

For nearly a week now, the Government has been listing reasons why people should vote. "Don't you want your problems to be addressed?" one ad asks. "Elect a candidate in the elections who will become your voice," the ad exhorts voters.Another front page ad reads "A golden opportunity has come for you to change your destiny."

The government has tried to ensure that the ads don't take on the tone of a counter-boycott campaign and anger the already agitated populace. The ads spell out that "vote is a democratic right" and "choose the right candidate".

Nevertheless, one ad published on November 1 stated: "It is time for constructive thinking and not destructive."

Heading: Cong, BJP adopt ‘social engineering’ formula - Indian Express
Content:
An advertisement for a job may be common, but in Kashmir, a national political party has sought candidates for the coming Assembly polls through advertisements in local newspapers.

The advertisement placed by the Janata Party in a local English daily carries a photograph of the party's national working president, Vijay Mallya. Calling all "interested candidates", the advertisement directs them to contact the state party president, Som Nath Dabgotra.

The party offers many incentives to prospective candidates. When this reporter contacted Dabgotra posing as an applicant, he said: "There are no losses, only gains. If you can spend Rs 5 lakh, the party will give you Rs 25 lakh. You will have personal security officers, you will get a car and the government can even provide you with accommodation". While a political background is not necessary, the candidates must be "financially sound".

However, when contacted later, Dabgotra told The Indian Express, that his party was not short of candidates. "We have not published this (advertisement) to seek candidates," he said. "We are contesting 52 to 60 seats. We have four candidates lined up for each Assembly seat. We wanted to publicise our contact number so that if somebody wants to reach us, he would know how to do so."

The first phase of Assembly elections in the state is just a fortnight away. This is the first time that a political party is seeking candidates through an advertisement in the local media.

Meanwhile, an anonymous candidate has published a similar advertisement seeking 20 people to run his election campaign. The eligibility criteria: "Kashmiri Muslims from Habba Kadal Assembly constituency".

The advertisement reads: "Urgently required 20 people, Kashmiri Muslims of Habba Kadal constituency to run election campaign Cell No 9797553020". The Habba Kadal constituency in Srinagar that has a substantial Kashmiri Pandit votebank is going to polls in the last phase on December 24.

Heading: Cong leaves 3 seats for NCP - Indian Express
Content:
Playing the social engineering card in Chhattisgarh, both the ruling BJP and the opposition Congress have not only fielded an equal number of tribal and women candidates but have also given due prominence to nominees of Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in the Assembly polls scheduled for November 14 and November 20.

Though the Assembly seats reserved for tribals was reduced to 29 from 34 in the latest de-limitation exercise, both the BJP and the Congress fielded 32 tribal candidates each - one each from three general constituencies as well to woo the tribals, which constitute 32 per cent of the state's 21 million population.

Both the parties have also made conscious efforts to win over the OBCs, which form 52 per cent of the state's population, by fielding them from several general constituencies. Among the OBCs, Sahu and Kurmi communities enjoy considerable political clout in many districts.

While the BJP has earmarked 26 seats for OBCs, eight for the Vaishya community and seven for Brahmins, the Congress has given 21 seats to OBCs, eight to Brahmins, seven to Kshatriyas and five to Vaishyas.

Both parties have fielded 10 women candidates each, giving 11.11 per cent representation to women in their list of candidates for the 90-member Assembly.

The BJP, with caste equations in mind, has fielded OBC candidates against prominent Congress leaders, including state Congress working president Satyanarian Sharma from Raipur (Rural), a constituency in the state capital. The party has also not fielded any candidate from the Sikh and Muslim communities. Instead, it has replaced two sitting Sikh legislators with a woman and an upper caste candidate.

Heading: Gaur’s widow to contest on BJP ticket - Indian Express
Content: The Congress in a seat sharing arrangement with the Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) for the Assembly elections in Chhattisgarh, has in its third list for 47 seats, released on Saturday, left three seats — Chandrapur, Samri and Manendragarh — for the NCP. Local Congress leaders in these constituencies have aired their resentment against the decision.The Congress confirmed on Sunday that former CM Ajit Jogi will contest the polls from Marwahi.

Heading: Prime witness fears for his life, blames police - Indian Express
Content:
Malini Gaur, at whose Indore residence Sadhvi Pragya Singh had stayed for days, will contest on BJP ticket from Indore-4 constituency. "She is a Sadhvi, I respect her," she told The Indian Express when asked about her association with the accused in the Malegaon blast case. The 47-year-old has never contested any election before and remained in the background while her husband Laxman Singh Gaur took the centerstage.

The former education minister, who represented the Indore-4 constituency, died in a road accident early this year. The Sadhvi had stayed in the family's new home for a long time after the minister's death.

Malini Gaur featured in the third list of candidates released by the BJP on Monday, when the BJP formally rushed to defend the Sadhvi saying there was no evidence yet against her. The Sadhvi was photographed along with BJP president Rajnath Singh and Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan, when they had gone to Gaur's residence to offer condolences.

On Monday afternoon, the mood was visibly different. BJP supporters thronged her house to congratulate her. She said the photograph had been misused to score political points because leaders from other parties had also visited her to offer condolences.

She said she was unsure if the family's closeness to the blast accused would go in her favour or against. "It's for the rivals to decide." She said she had campaigned for her husband and continued his unfinished work after his death.

Laxman Singh Gaur, a popular politician, was a staunch RSS follower. On getting the education portfolio, he had tried to make Sanskrit compulsory from Class I and introduced 'Guru Paad Pujan' wherein students were supposed to wash their teachers' feet on Teachers' Day.

A graduate, Malini Gaur runs a CBSE school on the Agra-Mumbai Road. After her husband's death, she had organised a convention of thousands of women to mobilise opinion on the Amarnath shrine board issue.

Incidentally, PWD Minister and official spokesman of the MP Government Kailash Vijayvargiya, who offered legal assistance to the Sadhvi and visited the family of Sham Sahu, another accused in the custody of Mumbai ATS, will contest from Mahu constituency.

Heading: Delhi chase shadows on a Sunny day - Indian Express
Content:
The prime witness in the recent serial blasts in Assam, who provided a vital description of two suspects for sketches made by the special probe team, is a haunted man today. Not only because of what he saw on October 30 but because the Assam Government has publicly announced his name as a witness, but has not provided him with any security.

The Express team on Monday tracked down fifty-five-year-old Pradip Konwar, a public prosecutor who saw two suspects near the car which exploded at the parking lot of CJM court. "We are all very scared. They did not provide me with protection. Instead, at a press conference they announced my name. What if the militants try and shoot me or my wife or my children?" a visibly shaken Konwar told The Indian Express.

Recounting that fateful day, Konwar stated that he entered the CJM csurt premises at around 10.30 am as usual. "I parked my car in the parking lot and got out. On the opposite side, I saw two men standing near a Maruti. As I looked at them they stared back at me. I felt there was something strangely suspicious, but ignored it," said Konwar. Thinking nothing further of it, Konwar went into the courtroom of the additional CJM in connection with some case. At around 11.15 am he heard a loud noise outside and rushed out.

Konwar then witnessed the rows of burning cars and charred and injured persons crying out for help. He called up the police and lent a hand in the rescue work. "I was busy in the rescue work and only after an hour I remembered those two persons. I do not know whether they are the culprits but it was strange for them to stand like that on a busy workday," added Konwar. According to Konwar one man was around 40 years old and was wearing kurta pyjama, while his companion seemed to be in his early 20s and was wearing a dark shirt and trousers. "The young man had a dark complexion and the older one had a beard," said Konwar.

Later, the police took his statement and he was summoned to the CID office a number of times. "I was called to the CID office and senior officers including the ADG spoke to me for long hours. I gave them the details of the two men. An artist drew sketches based on my details," added Konwar.

However, his trauma truly started after the IPG (Law and Order) Bhaskar Jyoti Mahanta held a press conference on November 1 and announced his name as the only eyewitness to have seen suspects and stated that sketches were being drawn. Konwar stays at Beltolla in Guwahati along with his wife Aparna who is a teacher in Rangiya College, and two children — daughter Sukanya is a higher secondary student at Srimanta Shankar Academy and son Supratim is a class IX student in Don Bosco school. The entire family is now living in fear. "I do not know why the IGP announced my name in the press conference. He even revealed that I am an advocate here. My wife has to go to teach and the children have to go out of the house for school. We all feel very insecure. What if something happens to them if I am right about the suspects?" added Konwar.

Meanwhile, Chief Minister Tarun Gogoi in a press conference announced that the sketches of the two suspects will be released shortly. "I have spoken to Konwar personally and sketches of suspects made with his description. This is all I can say right now," said Subhas Goswami, ADG CID. "Sketches are being prepared on the basis of several eyewitnesses and will be released in due time," said Hemanta Biswa Sharma, state Health Minister and Assam Government spokesperson.

Heading: ‘I hope many more hundreds will come’ - Indian Express
Content:
The first delivery was a bouncer from Pradeep Sangwan that was fended off deftly. Next ball, an inside edge that rolled dangerously close to the stumps. Then, sandwiched between two deliveries that were left alone, one ball touched a dead bat. And finally, the last ball of the over was tamely lobbed to first slip. The Yuvraj Singh show started 10 minutes before lunch, and ended with two minutes still left for the interval — six balls, eight minutes, no score.

Yuvraj was the first of his team mates to arrive at the ground on Monday morning, and remained at the Roshanara Club with the last batch that saw the covers coming on, and the outfield being invaded by members. But the left-hander, playing his first match for Punjab in two years, couldn't remain for long enough in the middle of the crease, the spot he so desperately needed to occupy.

On his dismissal, Yuvraj trudged slowly towards the pavilion, and while he remained the 'main event' thereafter for autograph hunters, his colleague Sunny Sohal revelled in the attention of national selector Yashpal Sharma with his maiden century that helped the visitors recover from a precarious 92 for 3 to a healthy 237 for 5 when play ended early due to fading light. Uday Kaul and Ankur Kakkar saw the team through the post-tea schedule for a sixth-wicket stand of 61 as Delhi lost the early initiative.

Sohal, coming in at number three after Ashish Nehra had sent Ravi Inder Singh's stumps flying, remained a nervous starter with the pitch offering ample justification for Delhi skipper Aakash Chopra's decision to field first. But once the sheen was taken off the new ball, and the ball replaced twice inside 26 overs, the lone right-hander in the top-four latched on to anything pitched up. He prospered in the middle session, belting 10 boundaries for his half-century and nine more in his next 50, as the wicket eased up considerably under the afternoon sun.

Sizzling Nehra

The Delhi bowlers bowled well in patches, but Nehra clearly stood out as someone belonging to a higher level of cricket. The lanky left-arm seamer started with an incisive spell with the new ball, and was probing throughout his other spells. The effort gave him scant rewards but generated ample admiration.

His understudy, Sangwan, was a touch guilty of overdoing the short stuff but doled out a lion-hearted performance nonetheless. He provided vital breakthroughs in his second spell, removing Ravi Inder Singh and Yuvraj after a change of ends.

Amit Bhandari bowled with zest but without any luck and together the pace attack asked questions, inducing seven outside edges that dropped frustratingly short of an extended slip cordon.

Seam-up Rajat Bhatia and leg-spinner Chetanya Nanda proved steady allies — the latter had Sohal for 110 at mid-on and skipper Pankaj Dharmani for 16 — but the lack of a specialist off-spinner against a team who have five left-handers didn't help Delhi's cause as the day wore on.

Chopra at helm

Chopra was quick to fish out the second new ball after 81.2 overs in a bid to get an extra wicket. His ability to shuffle his seam bowlers for short bursts — Nanda was pressed into service only in the 41st over — were good signs from a man wearing the captain's band for the first time. With the pitch proving a good host to the batsmen, the opening spells in the morning will once again be decisive as Punjab look to add to their first-innings tally. As things stand, the job is only half done for both sides.

Heading: Rahane, Sharma rescue Mumbai - Indian Express
Content:
Yuvraj Singh was supposed to be the star of the day but on Monday, it was Sunny Sohal, who shone bright for Punjab.

"I am very happy today. This is my first hundred and I hope that many more will come from my bat," Sohal said, though he admits to throwing away his wicket immediately after. "I played a bad shot and I am not proud of it. I wanted to clear the mid-on fielder but couldn't connect the ball well and I was caught. Guess I gave my wicket away," he added.

Sohal single-handedly pulled Punjab out of a difficult situation, after the rest of the top order misfired on a good batting surface. "Arun Paaji (coach Arun Kumar Sharma) and my team mates were happy for me, but I know our team's situation could have been better had I kept my end intact. A score of 237 isn't great after 80-odd overs," he said.

Unlike others, Sohal has no fond memories of the Indian Premier League. Sohal, who was part of the Kings XI Punjab team, said he did not benefit from the exposure. "There were so many players and chances were few and far between. I played two matches where I batted really down the order. I played a single delivery in one and six balls in the other," Sohal recalled.

Heading: Vijay, Abhinav plunder Maharashtra - Indian Express
Content:
Ajinkya Rahane and Rohit Sharma hit contrasting half-centuries to help Mumbai score a decent 293 for eight on the first day of their Ranji Trophy season opener against Rajasthan at the Cricket Club of India's Brabourne Stadium on Monday.

Mumbai skipper Wasim Jaffer won the toss and elected to bat but the decision appeared to have backfired after the hosts were reeling at 103 for three at one stage. The young pair of Sharma and Rahane, though, added 106 runs for the fourth-wicket to steady the innings. While Sharma made a brisk 62 off 84 deliveries, Rahane was more sedate and scored 73 off 148 balls.

It was after openers Sahil Kukreja and Jaffer failed to give the team a good start. Kukreja (5) fell to medium pacer Sumit Mathur when the score was 37. Rahane and Jaffer took the total to 103 but two quick blows — Jaffer and Amol Majumdar — forced Mumbai on the back foot.

Rahane and Sharma then settled down and initiated a recovery for Mumbai. They took the total past 200 when an unknown off-spinner Ashok Menaria, making his debut, scalped two in three balls to tilt the balance in the visitors' favour. After removing Sharma, Menaria got new batsman and veteran Sairaj Bahutule caught at first slip by Venugopala Rao. Mumbai were suddenly 209 for five.

Rahane too departed six runs later, trapped in front off paceman Pankaj Singh's delivery which kept a bit low. The next pair of Ajit Agarkar and Ramesh Powar then added 43 runs for the seventh-wicket to take the total beyond 250. Agarkar, who struck a clean six off Gajendra Singh, fell to Menaria for 22, while Powar scored a fighting 33 before getting out at the score of 276.

At stumps, Vinayak Samant was batting on 14 while giving him company was Usman Malvi (5).

Heading: Back again, smiling - Indian Express
Content:
There's something about Ravi Inder Singh that grabs headlines — albeit for all the wrong reasons. The Punjab opener made it to the playing XI during the Challenger Trophy last month before it was revealed that it was case of mistaken identity with Saurashtra left-arm spinner Ravinder Jadeja. It was only at the end of day's play that Punjab manager Arun Bedi pointed out the mistake — as matters stand now, Karan Goel made 37 while Ravi was dismissed early for 2.

Heading: ‘Let seniors decide when to call it quits’ - Indian Express
Content:
It was easy enough to miss it. Under the roar that enveloped the Ferozeshah Kotla on Sunday evening, hidden behind the broad-shouldered Anil Kumble's final goodbye, handicapped by lumps in the throat and misty eyes, and caught up in the whirlpool of emotions that flowed through India's favourite hunting ground, it was easy enough to miss the fact that for the first time in the last three weeks, Ricky Ponting was walking off the field with a broad smile on his face, not the irritable frown that seemed to have been plastered on his forehead.

The visiting Australians, depleted by retirements of their biggest giants, burdened by the legacy of the past two decades, had started off well enough in Bangalore where they had India on the mat for a good part of five days. But their inability to blast the door open despite wedging a fair bit of foot in there was seen as the first sign of changing fortunes.

Then came Mohali, where they were out-thought and out-fought; with bat, ball and, rather amusingly, in the field as well. Brett Lee and Ricky Ponting were having a go not at opposition batsmen but each other, leading to giggles that Greg Chappell had made an impact after all.

Over to Delhi, and they spent two hot days on the field, playing awestruck spectators as Gautam Gambhir and VVS Laxman composed distinctly different and equally effective double-hundreds. But instead of being crushed under a mountain of 613 runs, they suddenly, inexplicably, got up and dusted themselves off and started climbing again.

Chipping in

What would please Australia more than the fact that they got away from the third Test unscathed and alive in the series is the manner in which they got within 36 runs of India's total. Matthew Hayden conquered his impulse to butcher Zaheer Khan and dug in instead, Simon Katich managed to find the right blend of dogged defence and nudgy run-gathering, Ponting kept Ishant Sharma out, Michael Hussey was back to his usual, monstrous self and Michael Clarke made the most of his good fortune to round things off.

India got there with two double-tons, Australia with four fifties and a century. In Mohali, their batsmen could hardly put bat on ball; going to Nagpur, they're all in form. Even Lee bowled, even if in patches, like he used to.

And so, the visitors found their voice. Michael Clarke came out at the end of Day Four to point out that it was India who were being defensive. Ponting, at the end of the game, could've been forgiven for bringing out his best told-you-we-weren't-rubbish grin. "We had our backs to the wall from stumps on the first day," said the Aussie skipper.

"But I am proud with the way we stuck at it in this Test match. Our batting through the game has been terrific. We got the worst of the batting conditions on that (Kotla) track, but our application and our skills through the remaining three days have been pretty good. So there're some good things heading into Nagpur."

Still in the game

Despite this mini-resurgence, India will be hugely disappointed if they don't win this series. They fought well in Bangalore, didn't put a foot wrong in Mohali and, apart from some shoddy catching on the fourth day, did most things right in Delhi as well. A track with a bit more bite might've done the trick. A fit Harbhajan Singh could've made a difference. No cause for panic.

They'll do well to be wary though. The Australians might be a shadow of the all-conquering champions that strutted through the world over the last two decades but they haven't — though they did give that impression through the early part of the tour — forgotten how to play cricket.

Heading: Howzzat! Gilly admits he was wrong in claiming Dravid’s catch - Indian Express
Content:
Rejecting suggestions that he was under pressure from the cricket board to quit, Anil Kumble, who hung his boots on Sunday, said it was entirely his decision and there was no 'retirement scheme' for the senior cricketers.

"Nobody told me when to retire," Kumble said. "It was my own decision and there was no pressure. There is no retirement scheme, that's all rubbish."

However, the 38-year-old did express anguish over the increased media pressure on the 'seniors' even at the slightest hint of a slack in their form. He said the players were the best judge of their form and the decision as to when to call it a day should be left to them.

"It's not easy to go out and play for India and perform every time. People need to realise that," Kumble told CNN-IBN.

"It was not right to judge someone on the basis of one (bad) series (in Sri Lanka). We have performed right through our careers. It was just one series where we failed, but that doesn't make you a bad player. There's a lot of young talent coming in but you can just discard the experience and the quality. It's sad that people use harsh words, it is a bit disrespectful.

"All these (senior) players have played enough cricket to understand when is the right time for them to quit, let's leave it to them. Why do you need to take a call on someone else? Nobody likes to hang around if he's not contributing to the team.

"Yes, everybody wants to go on a high, everyone wants a fairytale ending but then you know when the time is up and my only request is please leave it to them," he said.

Thumbs up to Dhoni

On his successor Mahendra Singh Dhoni, Kumble said the future of Indian cricket was safe in the stumper's hand. "I think Dhoni has done exceptionally well in all forms of the game as a captain and I think we have a very able leader in him. It is the right time for him to take over being 1-0 up in the series and it will be great to finish the series on a winning note and then we have a home series coming up against England, which I am very confident that we will be able to win."

But wouldn't he regret not having led the team to the Border-Gavaskar Trophy? "It's not (about) my personal glory, I might have been the captain of the team. It is a team effort and what matters to me the most is India winning the trophy. If I am the captain or am not the captain, I am part of the squad and we are one up going into the last Test match. From here on we can only win the series."

Academic interest

Kumble also addressed the media in Bangalore after his first homecoming as a 'former' cricketer, and spoke about his life after retirement. On his future plans, Kumble said he is working towards opening an academy for budding cricketers. "There are plans to start an academy, not immediately but in a couple of months. The groundwork has already started. I take interest in photography as well so may be I will try my hand at that," he said.

Asked whether the captaincy came a bit too late for him, Kumble said, "Captaincy came at the right time. When you have played for 17 years, it's not possible to have captaincy for five years. Whatever is not in my control I am not worried, whatever happens, happens for good.

"I have performed really well. I have taken a decision at the right time. I am at peace after taking this decision. I want to take some time off now... it will be nice for a change."

Board to felicitate Kumble

Meanwhile, the BCCI has decided to felicitate Kumble besides Sachin Tendulkar, VVS Laxman and Sourav Ganguly at Nagpur on November 6, the first day of the fourth and final India-Australia Test.

"Kumble will also be honoured along with Tendulkar, Laxman and Ganguly," board and VCA president Shashank Manohar said.

Heading: ‘On-field spats don’t look good from sidelines’ - Indian Express
Content:
It's not just Indian cricketers that Adam Gilchrist has found faults with, in a frank confession the former Australia wicketkeeper has admitted he was wrong in claiming Rahul Dravid's catch in the fateful Sydney Test.

Gilchrist said he had wrongly appealed for Dravid's scalp after he genuinely thought the Indian had nicked the ball but defended himself by saying that he was not a "cheater" with "an ugly win-at-all-costs attitude".

"The Dravid decision was a howler, but to this day I would not have acted any differently. It happened very quickly, there was a noise, the tension was high, I thought he'd hit it. We all went up," he wrote in his autobiography True Colours.

"To feel the ball coming into my gloves at slightly deflected angle, having heard the noise, I wasn't 100 per cent sure of course; but there was a good chance he'd hit it, so I appealed.

"...I appealed for something which I genuinely thought was out, and then replays showed it wasn't. It may have come as a surprise to Peter Roebuck and other critics, but I was not perfect. I did not have slow motion, Hawkeye, hot-spot vision. I thought Dravid had hit it. I was wrong!" he admitted.

On the fifth day of the Sydney Test, Dravid had batted two and a half hours for 38 before he went forward to an Andrew Symonds off spinner which Gilchrist thought was edged to him.

"I went up, we all went up, and the umpire gave him out. Replays would show that the ball and his bat had grazed his pad, and he hadn't hit it. Peter Roebuck had a problem with me because of the manner of Rahul Dravid's dismissal," Gilchrist said.

The former stumper, in his book, took a dig at Sachin Tendulkar, hinting that the Indian maestro was a sore loser besides questioning the commitments of Sourav Ganguly and Harbhajan Singh during their 2004 series.

Gilchrist also said the happenings during India's trip Down Under in 2007-2008 tarnished Australia's reputation to the extent that his honesty too got dragged into the line.

"Now I was being accused of being a bad sport, for claiming the catch. This was great example of what some of my teammates had warned me about; that my principled stance on walking would be used to beat me with.

"...according to Roebuck and others, I was part of an ugly win-at-all-costs attitude. I dropped my standards to the point where I was, basically cheating."

Gilchrist felt the Sydney Test also had a bearing on how the third Test at Perth would go.

"There were crucial moments in Perth when we hesitated, and I felt it cost us initiative in the match... The Indians lapped it up in the field. Knowing that we were the ones under pressure for our behaviour, they went in hard and aggressive, thinking it would not matter what they did."

Heading: Yousuf takes U-turn again, rejoins ICL - Indian Express
Content:
Ricky Ponting has warned his team mates to be extra careful about their behaviour on the cricket field as it might look worse than it actually is from the sidelines.

"Some of those things don't look very good from the sidelines and us as players need to understand they can look worse from the sidelines than they might be on the field," Ponting said referring to some exchanges during the drawn third cricket Test against India at the Ferozeshah Kotla.

The match, which started with heated exchanges between Gautam Gambhir, Shane Watson and Simon Katich, also saw Mitchell Johnson

irking VVS Laxman on the fifth and final day.

Ponting defended Johnson, saying "There was no real malice from anything Mitchell had to say. "It was about some of the comments that VVS had made in the newspapers, to tell the truth. That was all he was talking about. The umpires spoke to me and said it happened three times in the over, I think, and it wasn't acceptable. So I spoke to Mitchell at the break and that was it."

Despite the regular incidents, Ponting said they were not a result of Australia's frustration at the inability to break through India.

"I'd like to think those things aren't getting to us on the field," he said. "We've got a pretty clear job to do."

Heading: Bitter Bond breaks free, says won’t play for NZ - Indian Express
Content:
Pakistan cricket authorities were in a state of shock after prolific batsman Mohammad Yousuf on Monday left for New Delhi to play in the Indian Cricket League (ICL), jeopardising his international career even as he was named in the national squad for the series against the West Indies.

Pakistan Cricket Board officials confirmed they have learnt from Yousuf's wife that he would be playing in the unofficial ICL, dealing a severe blow to the national team which has witnessed a series of defections to ICL in the recent years. "He didn't tell us anything about his plans. His leaving like this for India and confirmation he is going to play in the ICL has come as a shock to us," PCB's Director Cricket Operations Zakir Khan said in a hastily arranged press conference. Newly appointed Pakistan coach Intikhab Alam said Yousuf's sudden departure was hard to explain as he never got a chance to interact with him on his future with the national team.

"Until we get an official confirmation from Yousuf himself we can't say much right now. But if he has joined the ICL then he would be banned from all cricket in Pakistan," Zakir said.

Beaten in flight!

Travelling to India on the same flight with Yousuf was PCB director general Saleem Altaf, but even he had no inkling to the batsman's plans. "I asked him where he is going. He just told me he is going to India on a private visit and would return after two days," said Altaf.

Heading: More than just a title - Indian Express
Content:
Miffed with the way New Zealand Cricket ostracised him for joining the ICL, pacer Shane Bond says he will never play ODIs or Tests for his country again even if recalled to the side.

"I still enjoy playing cricket. I am having a great time with the game, which has given me a nice career and financial security as well. But I was hoping to play for my country at least for a couple of years more.

"I'm disappointed with the way my country's board treated me. I don't want to represent New Zealand any more," he said.

The 33-year-old decided to play in the ICL after international cricket of six years, causing the New Zealand board to terminate his contract. His decision to participate in the Twenty20 tournament in India has also affected his future in domestic cricket. "Despite clearing me for the tournament earlier, the cricket board later changed its mind and stepped back from their stand. I am quite disappointed with that."

Heading: I didn’t gift Lewis the title, says Glock - Indian Express
Content:
Lewis Hamilton's achievement in becoming Formula One's youngest world champion at the age of 23 is only part of something far more significant for the glamour sport.

The first and only black driver, with his roots in the island of Grenada and childhood on a working-class housing estate in Britain, has shattered a barrier every bit as intimidating as the one dismantled by Tiger Woods years earlier.

Interlagos, the dilapidated temple of Brazilian motor racing in a melting pot of a metropolis with a crowd more multi-racial than anywhere else in Formula One, could identify with Hamilton on Sunday despite their natural support for home hero Felipe Massa. So too could millions of others, previously unmoved and unrepresented, in a billion-dollar sport struggling to shake off an image as the playground of excess for a moneyed, white elite.

In a sport where all drivers look the same with their crash helmets on and where the only race that matters to most is the one on a Sunday afternoon, times are changing. Even now, though, the number of black mechanics in the paddocks can be counted on one hand. Narain Karthikeyan was the first Indian Grand Prix driver in 2005, and there have been several other Asians, but otherwise the sport has been markedly white.

"I feel like any of the other drivers that are out there that it is a dream for me to get to Formula One," Hamilton said before his sensational debut last year. "But what comes with it is that hopefully it can be of some influence, it can encourage other ethnic groups to get involved in the sport. It doesn't have to be just for one group of people, it can be for everyone. People that can relate to the path that I've taken will see that it's possible and will try also to get into the sport," he added.

McLaren support

Hamilton has been supported by McLaren for more than a decade, their money helping his obvious talent, but nothing else in his background remotely suggested he might emulate drivers such as Michael Schumacher and Ayrton Senna.

Hamilton's paternal grandfather, Davidson, emigrated from the West Indies in the 1950s to work on the daily grind of the London Underground system. His father, Anthony, worked for the British railway system while his mother Carmen was an employee in a care home.

Hamilton's parents divorced when he was two. It was only when the youngster stepped into a child's go-kart on a hard-earned family holiday in Spain that he was bitten by the motorsports bug. He had already made an appearance on a television children's show for his prowess with radio-controlled cars, a hobby he still enjoys with half-brother Nicholas.

Crash dummy

On the racetrack, Hamilton has been a winner in every series he has entered. His Formula One debut, alongside double world champion team mate Fernando Alonso, showed he was overawed by no reputation. Hamilton racked up nine podiums in a row at the start of 2007, taking back-to-back wins in Canada and the United States and ending the season as overall runner-up by a single point after blowing his chance to become the first rookie champion.

This year he has won a further five times and attracted applause, criticism and controversy in equal measure. His move to Switzerland drew flak before the season when he said it was to protect his privacy rather than the more evident tax reasons connected with a contract tying him to McLaren until 2012.

British newspapers derided him as a "Crash Dummy" at the Canadian Grand Prix in June when he rammed into the back of Kimi Raikkonen's stationary Ferrari, waiting for a red light to change at the pitlane exit.

There have also been truly memorable moments: the victory at Silverstone in the wet hailed as one of the sport's great performances after he lapped all but the second and third-placed finishers and won by more than a minute.

On Sunday, a year on from his agonising failure at Interlagos, it all came good as the first British champion since Damon Hill in 1996 stood on top of the world. As a record, it could stand for years to come.

Heading: Big guns hope to rebound on Tuesday night - Indian Express
Content:
Timo Glock has said Lewis Hamilton won the world drivers' championship by his own skills and not because of the German's tyre choice for the final laps of the Brazilian Grand Prix.

Glock opted to stay on dry-weather tyres as light rain fell in the closing stages of Sunday's race and though he did not lose too much time initially, the final lap proved crucial as Hamilton passed him in the last few hundred metres to finish fifth and win the title.

"It was a hard race. I tried my best to get some points for Toyota," Glock told Radio Five Live on Monday. "Six laps from the end I asked about the tyre situation and about the weather conditions and I said every time 'I'll stay out, one more lap, one more lap' and at the end I stayed out for the whole race.

"That last lap just cost us the chance to be in the top five, and in the end decided the world championship," added Glock, who finished sixth.

"I think at the end I didn't give the title to Lewis, I think they worked for that the whole year, and Felipe as well," he said. "They both did a really great job all year and in the end it was a dramatic finale."

Hill praises Hamilton

SILVERSTONE: Meanwhile Damon Hill, the last British Formula One champion before Hamilton, hailed Britain's newest Formula One champion and said the 23-year-old McLaren driver would be hard to stop now. "I think it's a tremendous result," the 1996 champion said.

"He's come out on top after nearly winning it in his first season. Youngest ever world champion, Britain's new world champion and first one for 12 years. He's put Britain back at the top and we are very proud of him," added Hill. "Lewis is a tremendous talent, a great ambassador for British motor sport and possibly one of the greatest drivers we have had. He has got a world championship in the bank and I think he is going to be difficult to stop from now on."

"Massa had the pace, he couldn't do anything about it but you know Lewis deserved the championship. That's what it comes down to, if you look at the whole year, he definitely deserved the championship," said 1979 champion Jody Scheckter.

Heading: How wristy Saina is getting better every day - Indian Express

Heading: FM may ask banks to cut rates - Indian Express
Content:
The racquet-grip goes a softer shade of baby-pink occasionally these days when Saina Nehwal plays. But the hand that rocks the shuttle is only gaining in power, if not yet in legend. The sheer force with which the Haryanvi hits her strokes — especially the forehand crosscourt smashes — is now the cornerstone of Nehwal's game.

At the level of the World Juniors, Nehwal's smash-winners, which usually outnumber her opponents', have sorted out both: weaker players such as Indonesian quarter-finalist Lindaweni Fanetri, leaving her unable to react as quickly as she'd like, or pugnacious ones like Chinese semi-finalist Shixian Wang by taking control of a rally, and swiftly upping the pace with quick kills.

A slow starter in the first game at most times, Nehwal never looked threatened in Pune since big leads were bridged with the smash, which coach Gopichand calls Saina's special shot from the back-court. What has evolved over the last two years — it's still work in progress — is the 18-year-old's judicious use of her weapon.

There's the aggression post a smash that alarms rivals and brings points in a clutch. But there's also the looming half-smash when opponents look vulnerable in the lane. "She has powerful smashes, and then she has the same action for a drop shot — where she checks her wrist at the very last moment. Because of her reputation of being big on power, it catches opponents off-position," comments Danish coach Jakob Hoei.

When the racquet-hand comes in quick with a steep angle, it opens up a lot of space in the front-court to deceive opponents. It's not uncommon to find Nehwal trailing until a quick signal from coach Gopichand gets the wrist working.

In her own league

Martin Andrew, England junior coach, who has watched Nehwal's progress over four years, believes she is in stark contrast to previous Indians. "Saina's way stronger and lasts longer in matches. She also uses corners well. Her movement can get more fluent and strong, and it'll be interesting to see if Asians can exploit her on speed. But I think she'll work her way around that."

Indeed, if there's anything that can hamper her power-play, it'll be her inability to reach the shuttle in time. "But she seems to be working on that. Also, she's cut down on her errors in the last year, making her a steadier player," says Dinesh Khanna, a TV commentator who's seen Nehwal's rise from national-domination to her amazing Olympics run.

Doubts over Nehwal's court coverage tend to get muffled owing to her superior upper-body fitness. "She's slow on her legs compared to the Chinese. But her strength is her hand," says Malaysian Gan Wye. "Her hand skill and wrist-control makes up for slower strides," he adds.

"Technically she might not match the Chinese or Koreans, but she plays with a very big heart. Its difficult to get her to crack," adds finalist Sayaka Sato, who despite trying a bag of quick-tricks in the second game, felt distinctly over-powered.

Areas of concern

Another opponent who wilted was Shih Han Hung of Chinese Taipei. "She might look tentative initially. But in her mind, she's very clear about how to dictate points," Hung says.

Saina's polished game, with her power-weapon weaved in, is credited to the fashion in which Gopichand has moulded it — three straight shots, one cross-court pattern. "Just the confidence he gives her is huge. Plus, she looks a player who follows tough regimens, and listens to her coach to the last consonant," England coach Andrew says.

But this world title does not stop Indonesian Athik Jauhari, who has been working with the juniors at Hyderabad, from pointing out some areas of concern. "Her movement's fine, it can get better. She's not bad at the net too, but sometimes her smashes need to be harder. Also, she struggles to pick deep drop shots and smashes coming to her left or right," he says, hinting at a stricter training regimen.

Heading: Slowdown pushes export growth to an 18-month low - Indian Express
Content:
Finance Minister P Chidambaram is likely to tell public sector banks to bring down interest rates in order to boost flow of credit to the industry in his meeting with PSU bank chiefs tomorrow. Despite the CRR cut, credit has not been flowing to the industry and the cost of credit continues to remain high. In a meeting with industry chamber chiefs on Monday, the finance minister said that would ask public sector banks to bring down interest rates to make cheaper credit available in the market.

He is also likely to discuss the big-picture issues related to growth of the economy with bank chiefs and what can be done to remedy the problem apart from taking direct measures to boost credit flow. The issue of structural deficiencies in growth may also be discussed.

"The finance minister assured us that he is going to persuade bankers to look at how to reduce interest rates ... He is meeting bankers tomorrow," Assocham president Sajjan Jindal told reporters after meeting Chidambaram. Besides Jindal, CII president K V Kamath and Ficci president Rajeev Chandrasekhar also attended the meeting with the finance minister. ICICI MD and CEO KV Kamath said, "We will review interest rates after watching the impact of the RBI decision on liquidity. The finance minister has said he will talk to PSU banks tomorrow."

"As a banker I say this: The government cannot actually on its part lower rates. The banks have to lower interest rates," he added.

Jindal said that the finance minister had assured industry that there would be enough liquidity in the system so that demand flow starts and the situation like the zooming up of call money rates to 21-22 per cent, as happened on Friday last, would not be allowed to recur.

When asked whether the RBI is expected to take more measures to infuse liquidity, Jindal said, "Hundred per cent. On Saturday, the RBI released more liquidity. Probably, over the next couple of days, the authorities are going to watch and then they will take the next step," he added.

After having released Rs 1,85,000 crore through a slew of measures in the past few weeks, the RBI on Saturday announced measures like a one per cent cut in the cash reserve ratio and statutory liquidity ratio. It also announced a cut in the short-term lending rate, the repo rate, which would further inject Rs 85,000 crore in the economy.

The finance minister is also keenly working on how to reduce the impact on SMEs, which are facing credit shortage. Jindal said the meeting primarily discussed the issues faced by these enterprises. "The FM is worried about the SME sector. He wants to fix their problems," he said.

Once liquidity eased, demand would be generated across the industry —SMEs or large scale enterprises, he added. Even the housing sector will see demand. According to Jindal, the FM said the housing sector must be revived since it would create demand for other sectors as well.

Heading: ATF prices cut again, fares may stand - Indian Express
Content:
India's export growth plunged to an 18-month low in September this year on account of the softening demand for Indian exports in developed markets, according to official trade data released by the commerce ministry today. Total exports in September amounted to $13.75 billion, a year-on-year growth of only 10.4 per cent despite the sharp depreciation in the rupee over the last one year, which has fuelled Indian export demand significantly over the recent past. However, export growth over the April-September period of this year was substantially higher at 30.9 per cent primarily due to robust growth over the previous months. Total exports over this period amounted to $94.97 billion, up from $72.56 billion over the same period last year.

Trade analysts believe such disappointing figures at this time of the year, when goods are shipped to developed countries for the upcoming holiday season, does not augur well for Indian exports. "If exports are registering such a poor growth at this time of the year, it wouldn't be a surprise if growth turns negative over the next few months," Ajay Sahai, director-general of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO) told The Indian Express.

Apart from this, the problems of insufficient liquidity and tight credit supply are also adding to exporters' woes. "Pre- and post-shipment credit of 90 days does not suffice any more," he added. "Bulk orders from buyers in developed countries have almost ceased and exporters have no alternative but to hold large inventories of their supplies while they wait for further orders." The silver lining, however, was the decline in the trade deficit from almost $14 billion in August to $10.6 billion in September. This was primarily because of the sharp fall in international crude oil prices over the past few weeks. Though the oil import bill was still quite high at $9 billion as against $5.8 billion in September last year, it had shrunk from the $11-billion mark in August.

Non-oil imports, which largely comprise industrial inputs, too, grew at a healthy rate of 36.2 per cent to reach $15.28 billion, a sign that Indian production is still holding strong.

Heading: The man who will save capitalism from the capitalists - Indian Express
Content:
Cash-strapped airlines today got another breather when state-run oil firms further cut aviation turbine fuel (ATF) prices but they remained non-committal on slashing fares.

Oil firms cut ATF prices today by up to Rs 2,100 per kilolitre on top of the 17 per cent reduction announced last week. ATF in Delhi will cost Rs 44,965.70 per kl with effect from midnight tonight, a four per cent cut over the present Rs 47,017.93 per kl, an industry official said.

The reduction followed government exempting the fuel from payment of 5 per cent customs or import duty. Airlines, however, did not immediately say if the overall 20 per cent reduction (Rs 11,482.10 per kl) in jet fuel prices in three days would result in lowering of fares. Some of the airlines said they were "studying" the impact. They had reacted the same way when Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum had from November 1 cut ATF price in Delhi by Rs 9,429.87 per kl to Rs 47,017.93 per kl, in line with fall in international oil prices.

Heading: WHAT India Inc WANTS - Indian Express
Content:
Raghuram G Rajan, appointed as the honorary economic adviser to Prime Minister Manmohan Singh today, believes India must go for full capital account convertibility, reduce state control in banks, and pursue a monetary policy that focuses exclusively on inflation management. In his report on liberalising India's financial sector, he had actually detailed the sequence of reforms for the government.

At a time when India is grappling with the impact of the global credit crisis, Rajan's appointment is significant given his career-long ideological position of the need for free market economies that are necessarily governed by dexterous government regulation. Back in 2006, Rajan was among the few economists who presciently suggested the reason for higher risk tolerance and a brave new world of low volatility and high asset prices was the skewed incentive structure for financial market participants.

Born in Bhopal, Raghuram Rajan studied at some of the world's most prestigious universities: graduation in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi; an MBA from the Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad; and a PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

After a brief stint in Tata Administrative Services, he taught at the University of Chicago, the Stockholm School of Economics, Northwestern University and MIT.

In 2003, Rajan was awarded the inaugural Fischer Black Prize by the American Finance Association for contributions to finance by an economist under 40. In the same year, he became not only the youngest individual, but also the first from a developing nation to become the economic counselor and director of research of the IMF. In addition to being a director at the ISB, Hyderabad and an adviser to Sebi, Rajan teaches at the University of Chicago where he is the Joseph L. Gidwitz Professor of Finance. His research is broadly on the role of institutions in fostering economic development.

Rajan is a believer in an ideological middle ground between hard right-wingers and the Marxists. In the book Saving Capitalism from the Capitalists that he co-authored with Luigi Zingales, he proposes the theory that while the absence of rules can make the playing field uneven, too many rules of the wrong kind can have exactly the same effect. While he is evidently aware of class issues, he rejects the Marxist view that capitalism is intrinsically unstable. Rajan was deeply critical of the loan-waiver scheme, and had said it would destroy the credit culture of the country.

Cleaning up, step by step

Low-hanging fruit

• Unique national ID and no-frills savings account for all households

• Financial ombudsman

• Scrapping STT, allowing FIIs in currency & interest rate derivatives

Technically simple but difficult to implement

• Monetary policy that focuses only on inflation

• Freeing bank branching

• Full capital account liberalisation

Technically difficult & politically controversial

• Reducing govt control in financial sector institutions

• Reforms of the regulatory framework

Heading: Sensex past 10K, rupee strengthens - Indian Express
Content:
In a meeting with the Prime Minister to assess the impact of global meltdown on India, industry captains asked him to inject enough liquidity and ensure slashing of interest rates to drive the economy on a growth trajectory.

Raise FDI cap in manufacturing, ease liquidity crunch further

Sunil Bharti Mittal, CMD Bharti Group

Bailout mutual fund and non-bank finance companies, remove interest rate ceiling on NRI deposits

K V Kamath, MD & CEO, ICICI Bank Limited

Realty sector saw a decline of 30 per cent in the last one year; lower consumer finance interest rates

K P Singh, Chairman, DLF Group

Increase flow of credit to SMEs and exporters, raise govt spending in infrastructure projects to spur employment

Sajjan Jindal, Vice Chairman & MD, JSW Steel Ltd

Raise FDI cap in aviation, insurance and retail; cut CRR and Repo rate further as zero trickle down effect as of now

Rajeev Chandrasekhar, President, FICCI

Heading: Union Bank cuts PLR by 50 bps; ICICI to decide soon - Indian Express
Content:
Buoyed by cuts in repo rate and reserve requirements by the Reserve Bank of India over the weekend, the BSE Sensex rose 550 points, or 5.62 per cent, to close above 10,000 at 10,337.68 on Monday. The rupee also soared by 1.6 per cent to 48.64 against the dollar as broad dollar weakness and hopes for fresh capital inflows boosted the sentiment.

With this, the market has staged a good rebound after a recent steep fall. From a low of 8,509.56 on October 27, 2008, the BSE Sensex has risen 1,828 points or 21.48 per cent in four trading sessions.

"The RBI move to cut CRR, SLR and repo rates, Sebi's decision to increase tenure for lending and borrowing of stocks and firm Asian stocks boosted the domestic bourses," said a BSE dealer. The rally was led by gains in capital goods, banking, auto and realty stocks. The market also got support from the Prime Minister assurance to business leaders that government will take measures to protect growth.

He also said the government was working closely with other countries to ensure coordinated policy action for the containment of the global financial crisis. Investors were also enthused by Finance Minister P Chidambaram's statement that he would ask PSU banks to bring down interest rates.

Lower rates boost corporate bottomline by way of lower borrowing costs. The RBI move will ease a growing cash squeeze, spur faltering economic growth and fend off damage from the global financial crisis. FIIs which bought shares worth $250 million on Friday were buyers on Monday as well as they invested another $80 million.

The Sebi decision to extend the tenure for lending and borrowing of stocks is aimed making the domestic SLB mechanism more robust and increase liquidity in the secondary markets. While short selling shares, the SLB mechanism facilitates the sellers to borrow stocks and cover his position. Naked short sales are not allowed in India.

European shares rose on Monday to track gains on the Wall Street and in Asia, as investors hoped recent worldwide steps to stem the financial crisis and likely rate cuts in Europe this week would calm market nerves. Asian stocks edged up for a fifth straight day on Monday on hopes policy efforts so far to dampen the impact of the financial crisis would ultimately take hold, though data still painted an ugly picture of the global economy. Key benchmark indices in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore and South Korea rose by between 1.44% to 3.93%.

The rupee rose to its highest in a fortnight on Monday amidst hopes for fresh capital inflows. The rupee ended at 48.64/65 per dollar, its strongest since October 17 and gaining 1.6 per cent from 49.44/46 at close on Friday. However, the rupee has still shed about 19 per cent so far in 2008 and hit a record low of 50.29 last week.

The dollar has weakened against all major currencies and, moreover, the RBI measures to infuse liqudity helped the stock market move up. The rupee may not move up much, 48.40 should hold, but the market will continue to remain very volatile, dealers said.

Heading: Market regulator sees no problem with FMP investment strategies - Indian Express
Content:
After interest rate cuts by Punjab National Bank and IDBI Bank, state-owned Union Bank of India on Monday reduced its benchmark prime lending rate (BPLR) by 0.5 per cent to 13.5 per cent with immediate effect. ICICI Bank Managing Director K V Kamath said the bank would review interest rate in the next few days.

The rate cut will be applicable for all PLR-related loans including auto, home and corporate loans, UBI said. The move follows the Reserve Bank slashing its key rates such as cash reserve ratio (CRR), statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) and short-term lending rate (repo) with a view to stabilise the liquidity conditions in the banking system.

Other banks, including the largest lender SBI, are also likely to take a call on their interest rates in the coming days.

Finance Minister P Chidambaram will meet heads of public sector banks on Tuesday in the backdrop of series of measures taken by the Reserve Bank to ease money supply. The banks are expected to be asked by the government to consider cut in interest rates following a slew of measures taken by the RBI to inject liquidity into the cash-starved banking system.

"We will review interest rates after watching the impact of the RBI decision on liquidity. Finance Minister P Chidambaram has also said he will talk to PSU banks tomorrow," Kamath, who is also the President of CII, said after meeting Chidambaram along with heads of FICCI and Assocham.

"The government cannot actually on its part lower rates. The banks have to lower interest rates," Kamath said. Pointing out that there is a need for a steep cut in interest rates if the country has to achieve a growth of 8 per cent, Kamath said "it is the interest rate that will drive this growth."

Heading: American Express sacks ‘less than 100’ workers - Indian Express
Content:
Though the real estate sector got the roughest treatment in the market turmoil, the market regulator does not think there is any inherent problem with the sector.

"We do not look at sectors in isolation and have no issues with real estate being the underlying asset in fixed maturity plans (FMPs) of mutual fund houses," said a highly placed official in the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi).

When asked whether the Sebi would limit exposure of FMPs in the real estate sector, Sebi executive director R K Nair said, "The market regulator is not into micro-management of offers. While vetting an offer document of a mutual fund house we only ascertain that there have been proper disclosures. When an FMP is offered to an investor, the underlying asset is pre-negotiated and the exit routes are also declared."

Nair attributed the high redemption pressure in FMPs to the higher rate of interest given by commercial banks. "Corporate houses, who are the major investors in FMPs, find it more attractive to keep their money in banks who are providing 11-12 per cent."

However, he said that mutual fund houses should, in their own interest, make sure that the investors don't leave them before a stipulated time. "All FMPs are close-ended except for the liquid schemes, even in these schemes MF houses can negotiate with an investor at the time frame for exiting. It is a business decision between the two parties and the fund managers of MF houses invest in assets based on their ratings by agencies. The regulator does not look at sectors with different views and is not into micro-managing matters," Nair said.

The regulator believes that if there is high risk in a particular investment, it should be properly disclosed in the offer document. "We want the disclosures by fund houses to be of international standard and won't resist from taking action if we find a fault in that. It is very important that fund houses declare the underlying assets of FMPs in no uncertain terms," Nair said.

No plan to limit FMPs' exposure in realty

•Sebi has no issues with realty being the underlying asset in fixed maturity plans of MF houses, says official.

• Says while vetting an offer document of an MF house, Sebi only ascertains that there have been proper disclosures

Heading: European bank profits evaporate - Indian Express
Content:
Global travel and payment services major American Express today said that it has sacked less than a hundred employees in India to restructure its workforce as part of its global strategy.

"The number is less than a hundred," American Express India's Public Affairs and Communications Director Vibha Bajaj told PTI.

Earlier, there were reports of about 200 India-based employees of the American company having been handed over pink slips by the management of India operations.

The company had said in a statement that "reduction will occur throughout the company and across business units, markets and staff groups, primarily focusing on management and other positions that do not interact directly with customers".

Those laid off, according to the information available, were mainly working in the back offices of the company in Delhi and Bangalore, sources said.

When asked whether the laid off employees included manager- and senior manager-level officials, Bajaj answered in the affirmative but she did not respond to a query whether the number included director-level officers as well.

Heading: Airlines may be able to pay AAI in EMIs - Indian Express
Content:
Profits evaporated at top European banks on Monday and authorities worldwide pressed on with efforts to temper a recession that policymakers said had become reality for much of the globe. The European Commission said the 15-nation euro zone was in a technical recession and economic growth would come to a virtual standstill next year. It called for coordinated action.

In Jerusalem, Richmond Federal Reserve Bank President Jeffrey Lacker said the US economy was certainly contracting. Data last week showed it shrank at a 0.3 percent annual rate in the third quarter, its sharpest squeeze in seven years. French bank Societe Generale reported an 83.7 percent drop in third-quarter net profit but said it was strong enough to withstand the global financial crisis.

Germany's second-biggest bank, Commerzbank, said it would take an 8.2 billion euro capital injection from the state and another 15 billion to secure refinancing. It posted a third quarter net loss of 285 million euros.

Britain's biggest home lender HBOS Plc raised its hit from the value of risky assets and bad loans to over 5 billion pounds ($8.14 billion) as its takeover partner Lloyds TSB predicted a sharp fall in profits. Lloyds stepped in to buy HBOS in a government-brokered deal after HBOS was hit by the crisis and concerns about its exposure to Britain's weakening housing market.

The United States, Germany, France and Britain have offered to inject capital into their banks to prevent systemic meltdown.

Heading: Global crisis plunges Europe into recession - Indian Express
Content:
Troubled airlines now have another reason to cheer, after a slew of measures taken by the government to keep them afloat. As a part of its efforts to bail out the sector from the current crisis, the government is now considering a proposal for the payment of airlines' dues towards the Airport Authority of India (AAI) in the form of interest-free monthly instalments.

In fact, the civil aviation ministry is working on the proposal as the matter is likely to come up before the committee convened to look into the current financial crisis in the sector under cabinet secretary K M Chandrasekhar next week. The committee has on board the oil and petroleum ministry and the finance ministry apart from the civil aviation ministry.

"The airlines are going through a difficult period. They have not been able to pay the AAI dues. We are looking at waiving off the interest on payments which have been defaulted on, in addition to the possibility of monthly payment of outstanding dues," said an official, close to the development. However, he also pointed out that this will mean a significant loss to AAI. Recently, oil companies allowed a six-month window to airlines to clear their dues, estimated to be around Rs 2,500-2,800 crore, by March 2009 in six equated interest-free monthly instalments.

According to the government data, the domestic carriers owe a substantial amount to the AAI. The top two domestic carriers — Kingfisher Airways and Jet Airways — account for around Rs 255 crore and Rs 36 crore respectively. State-carrier National Aviation Company of India Ltd (NACIL) has outstanding dues of Rs 653.10 crore. Spice Jet, Paramount, Indigo and Go Air owe Rs 21 crore, Rs 10 crore, Rs 5 crore and Rs 7.98 respectively. Similarly, foreign airlines have outstanding dues of around Rs 158 crore, taking the total uncleared amount, payable to AAI, to Rs 1,170 crore.

AAI charges airlines for providing services like landing, parking, terminal and route navigation in addition to renting out land and building to airlines for providing engineering facilities and office space. Typically, airlines are to settle their dues within 15 days, a period which has been breached by most, informed the official.

Heading: Fed’s Lacker says US in a recession - Indian Express
Content:
The global financial crisis is pushing the whole European Union into recession, official forecasts said on Monday, as South Korea unveiled its own 8.5 billion dollar stimulus package against the turmoil.

The European Commission forecast a short shallow recession for the 27-nation EU, predicting the bloc's combined economy would shrink 0.1 percent in both the third and fourth quarters of 2008.

"The economic horizon has now significantly darkened as the European Union economy is hit by the financial crisis that deepened during the autumn and is taking a toll on business and consumer confidence," said EU Economic Affairs Commissioner Joaquin Almunia.

The forecast by the EU's executive arm also said the economy of the 15 nations that use the euro shrank 0.2 in the second quarter and is set to contract by 0.1 percent in both the third and fourth quarters. It is the first time that the eurozone has slumped into recession — which economists broadly define as two consecutive quarters of economic contraction — since the single currency was introduced in 1999. In the face of sharply slowing growth, the commission forecast unemployment would return as a major headache after a steady decline in recent years.

It predicted that the unemployment rate in the eurozone would creep up from a record low of 7.2 percent in March to 8.7 percent in 2010. The impact of the slowdown was highlighted by a year-on-year 7.3 percent fall in new car sales in France, according to official figures for October.

The motoring sector employs, directly or indirectly, 10 percent of the French workforce, and companies have ordered massive production cuts.

Heading: Manufacturing crash adds to global gloom - Indian Express
Content: Richmond Federal Reserve Bank President Jeffrey Lacker said on Monday the US economy was definitely in a recession but he believed it would be fairly moderate in size. "We are in a contraction. Up until the summer it was a fairly mild recession," Lacker, who will become a voting member of the Fed's interest rate-setting committee next year, told reporters after a speech at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. "I think it's definitely a recession at this point. How deep, how steep, and long it's going to be is uncertain," he said.

Heading: CEOs and famous investors hit hard by market dive - Indian Express
Content:
US factory activity contracted sharply in October, falling to its lowest in 26 years as the financial crisis ravaged the world's largest economy and its trading partners around the globe.

The one bright spot in the report was that its main gauge of inflation, the prices paid measure, recorded its biggest one-month drop ever. This should allow the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates low to fight off what many fear will be a deep recession.

"Pretty grim. It means we're in a recession, it's as simple as that... a pretty solid manufacturing recession," said Robert Macintosh, chief economist at Eaton Vance Corp in Boston. "The question is, 'How long or deep is it going to be?'" The Institute for Supply Management said its index of national factory activity fell to 38.9 in October from 43.5 in September. That was well below the 50 level separating contraction from expansion, and a reading below 40 is exceptionally weak.

Economists had expected a reading of 41.5, according to the median of forecasts in a Reuters poll.

On Wall Street, stocks briefly turned lower after the weaker-than-expected data, but later eked out modest gains. The dollar trimmed its gains versus the yen.

Heading: Pakistan warns US General Petraeus against missile strikes - Indian Express
Content:
Here's something that might provide a bit of solace amid the plunging values in your retirement accounts: Warren Buffett is losing lots of money, too. So are Kirk Kerkorian, Carl Icahn and Sumner Redstone.

They are still plenty rich, but their losses — some on paper and others actually realized — illustrate how few have been spared in today's punishing market when even big-name investors, corporate executives and hedge-fund titans are all watching their wealth evaporate.

The portfolio damage for some of these high-flyers has soared to billions of dollars in recent months. And they can't just blame the market's downdraft — some did themselves in with badly timed stock purchases or margin calls on shares bought with loans.

"It's always hard to beat the market no matter who you are," said Robert Hansen, senior associate dean at Dartmouth's Tuck School of Business. "But when the ocean waters get that rough, it is hard for any boat to avoid getting swamped."

As stocks have plunged, so have the value of chief executives' equity stakes in their own companies. The average year-to-date decline is 49 percent for the corporate stock holdings of CEOs at 175 large US companies, according to new research by compensation consulting firm Steven Hall & Partners.

Topping that list is Buffett, who has seen the value of equity in his company, Berkshire Hathaway, fall by about $13.6 billion, or 22 percent, so far this year, to leave his holdings valued at $48.1 billion.
